Why GTLB now? What story is the market telling?
 
GitLab (GTLB) is not a new name — it is an old platform being repriced. The code repo is being built into the Duo Agent Platform: from a tool humans use to write code into the execution layer where agents write, review, secure, and ship software. Price is about $46.5, market cap about $7.9B. Last 7 days about +8%, last month about +32–36%, 52-week range $18.73–$52.38. There is only one near-term focus: Q2 after the US close tonight (call at 4:30 p.m. ET). The software-agent tape is hot this week — PATH reports Thursday — and GTLB is the first name on that line to print numbers.
 
  1. Business snapshot A DevSecOps platform covering plan, code, security, and operations. The market cares about one thing: it sits on the path from code generation to production. The faster agents write code, the more the platform is worth.
Core products:
  • GitLab platform: repo + CI/CD + security scanning, one suite instead of a pile of point tools.
  • GitLab Duo / Duo Agent Platform: the assistant upgraded into orchestrated coding agents for write, patch, compliance, and delivery.
  • Agent Catalog: first-party agents plus Claude, OpenAI, Gemini, and other external agents.
  • Dedicated / government cloud: single-tenant and compliance-heavy large accounts.
Key figures (already reported):
  • Last quarter (Q1 FY27) revenue about $264M, up about 23% YoY.
  • TTM revenue about $1.0B, gross margin still high (around 85%).
  • Q1 restructuring: roughly 14% headcount cut and exit from about 22 countries, costs redirected to AI.
  • Tonight’s Q2 Street ballpark: revenue about $273M, EPS about $0.18.
  • Short interest about 9% of float — if the print is clean, the after-hours move will not be small.
The company is shifting from “dev-tool seats” to an operating system for software delivery in the agent era.
  1. Expectation gap What the market already believes:
  • Up more than 30% in a month, RSI stretched — tonight is a check, not a launch.
  • Consensus target around $39, below the current price. The Street is not chasing.
  • Growth in the low-20s against an agent multiple: a soft guide gets labeled “story ahead of numbers.”
  • Post-restructure execution, large-account renewals, and whether AI attach actually bills are still unproven.
What may be different:
  • The seat is earlier than “another AI plugin.” Agent-generated code still has to land in a repo, pass the pipeline, and clear security. GitLab collects the toll on that execution layer.
  • If the call quantifies Duo Agent (adoption, revenue contribution, large-account penetration), the tape can re-rate from tool stock to agent-platform stock.
  • The restructuring cut is already in. Cleaner expense lines mean more elasticity in margin and guidance than in the top line.
  • PATH prints Thursday on the same theme. GTLB sets the tone tonight.
  1. Catalysts
  • Already done: Q1 growth held, restructuring to fund AI, Duo Agent / Agent Catalog rollout.
  • Tonight (Sep 1 after the US close) Q2: revenue/ARR growth, net retention, Duo/Agent commentary, next-quarter and full-year guide. This is the only hard catalyst this week.
  • Near-term follow-through: Agent platform demos and customer stories in September; large-account and government deals.
  • Next earnings around early December. rDOCU also reports Thursday night — same-sector beta, do not stack both full size.
  1. Key levels Setup: agent execution-layer narrative + earnings tonight + mid-cap size. Trade it as a high-level verification tape, not as a “just doubled off the lows” trend.
  • Support: $44–45 (pre-earnings shelf); stronger support $42, then $40.
  • Near-term targets: hold and $50 is in play; above that the 52-week high at $52.4.
  • Invalidation: a decisive break of $42 = squeeze-out plus a failed verification. Do not hold the restructuring story through that.

Fundamentals and valuation

Tesla's core focus has gradually shifted from simple vehicle sales growth to whether the automotive business can stabilize its base while Robotaxi, FSD, and Optimus begin to generate real commercial revenue.
The automotive business showed a clear recovery in 2026. Deliveries reached 358,000 units in Q1 and surged to a record 480,000 units in Q2, bringing first-half deliveries to roughly 838,000 units. However, Q2 automotive gross margin was only 16.3%, and quarterly free cash flow fell to -$1.1 billion as capital expenditure on AI, Robotaxi, and robotics increased rapidly. Active FSD subscriptions grew 56% year-over-year, indicating rising software penetration, but at this stage, the automotive business still bears the responsibility of providing the cash flow and scale foundation for Tesla's AI strategy.
For the automotive and energy storage businesses over the next three years, the sell-side consensus estimates compiled for Tesla are roughly as follows:
Metric 2026E 2027E 2028E
Vehicle deliveries 1,650,000 1,820,000 2,070,000
Energy storage deployment 57.9 GWh 79.8 GWh 99.9 GWh
What will truly determine growth elasticity for 2027–2028 are these three new businesses: Robotaxi/Cybercab, FSD, and Optimus.
 

This week's strategy

Direction: Event-driven bullish bias, pending confirmation from the September 3 Cybercab event.
Key levels:
  • First support: $360
  • Second support: $353–355
  • First resistance: $375
  • Medium-term resistance: $400 (200-day moving average)
  • Upside target: $410–420
TSLA surged 5.5% on August 31 to $367.95, reclaiming the 50-day moving average near $360, as the market began pricing in the September 3 Cybercab event ahead of time. $375 marks the first confirmation level for a short-term strength shift, while $400 represents the key breakout level with medium-term directional significance.
(1) Bullish scenario: bullish bias
Trigger conditions:
  • The Cybercab event delivers clear commercialization progress, including expanded autonomous driving scale, accelerated production, expansion into new cities, or a clearer Robotaxi economic model
  • The stock breaks above and holds $375
  • The stock further holds above the 200-day moving average (around $400)
Strategy:
  • After breakout confirmation, focus first on $400
  • First target: $410–420
  • It is better to wait for confirmation of a breakout above $375 rather than chasing gains continuously ahead of the event
(2) Neutral scenario: range-bound
The Cybercab event largely meets market expectations but lacks new quantifiable targets, with Robotaxi continuing its gradual expansion.
The stock is more likely to consolidate within the broad $350–400 range, with the area near $360 remaining the short-term dividing line between bulls and bears. Existing positions can continue to be monitored, but it is not advisable to actively increase positions within the $375–400 resistance zone.
(3) Bearish scenario: bearish bias
Trigger conditions:
  • The event content leans toward long-term vision again, with actual Robotaxi scale, regulatory progress, or Cybercab mass-production pace falling short of market expectations
  • The previous 18% gain in August is quickly given back
  • The stock breaks below $353–355

Fundamentals and valuation

Broadcom is currently still driven by two main lines: the rapid expansion of custom AI accelerators (XPU) and the AI networking business, plus the high-margin software cash flow from VMware. FY2026 Q2 revenue reached $22.2B, up 48% year-over-year, with an adjusted EBITDA margin of 69%. Of this, AI semiconductor revenue was $10.8B, up 143% year-over-year. The company had previously guided Q3 AI semiconductor revenue to rise further to $16B, up more than 200% year-over-year, indicating that ASIC demand from hyperscale customers such as Google is still in a phase of rapid expansion.
The Q3 earnings report, due after market close on September 2, will be the most important short-term catalyst. The market currently expects quarterly revenue of about $29.4B and adjusted EPS of about $3.24. Since the company has already given guidance for $29.4B in revenue, simply meeting expectations would have limited impact. The market is more focused on whether AI revenue exceeds $16B, and whether management continues to raise its outlook for 2027 AI revenue and new customer additions. The options market currently implies a roughly 7% move in the week following the earnings report.
From a medium- to long-term valuation perspective, AVGO is currently trading at around $370. The latest consensus estimates from MarketScreener show:
 
Fiscal year Revenue EPS Implied P/E
FY2026E $106.1B $9.01 Approx. 41x
FY2027E $173.4B $16.51 Approx. 22x
FY2028E $234.0B $22.33 Approx. 17x
Broadcom's fiscal year ends around November each year. The current FY2026 valuation is still on the high side, but if AI revenue materializes as expected in 2027–2028, earnings growth could quickly digest the valuation. In other words, the current share price already reflects a fairly high premium for 2026's high growth, so what really determines the mid-term upside is whether XPU customer expansion and AI revenue can continue to be revised significantly higher in 2027. The latest 12-month forward P/E in the market is about 32x, notably lower than MRVL's level of about 58x.

Earnings trading strategy

Direction: neutral to slightly bullish, awaiting confirmation from results and guidance.
Key levels:
  • First support: $364–360
  • Strong support: $343
  • First resistance: $382–383
  • Upside target: $410–420
  • Stronger target: $430
(1) Bullish scenario: leaning bullish
Trigger conditions:
  • Q3 revenue and EPS clearly beat $29.4B and $3.24
  • AI revenue above $16B
  • Management continues to raise its outlook for Q4 and 2027 AI business
  • Share price breaks above and holds $395
Strategy:
  • First target: $410–420
  • After a further breakout, the target is around $430
  • Existing positions can be held; if a pullback to $395 holds, consider adding in the direction of the trend
(2) Neutral scenario: range-bound
Q3 results largely in line with expectations, AI revenue around $16B, but management does not meaningfully raise its outlook for future AI revenue.
This outcome would broadly match expectations, and the share price would more likely continue digesting its valuation between $350 and $395. Around $380–385, chasing the rally offers little value; it would be better to wait for support around $360, or wait for a genuine breakout above $395 before confirming direction.
(3) Bearish scenario: leaning bearish
Trigger conditions:
  • AI revenue falls short of expectations
  • Next-quarter guidance comes in weak, or management signals slowing order growth from major customers
  • Share price falls below $343

1. Investment Snapshot

Broadcom (AVGO.US) will report fiscal third-quarter 2026 results after the U.S. close on September 2, 2026. Management has guided quarterly revenue to about $29.4 billion (+84% YoY), including AI semiconductor revenue of about $16 billion (over +200% YoY). Street consensus is roughly $29.2–$29.5 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of about $3.22 (+90.5% YoY). Ahead of the print, JPMorgan kept an Overweight rating and a $580 price target, arguing the quarter should come in solid and that Q4 guidance is more likely to set the stock. Shares have pulled back meaningfully from the highs, options imply about an 8% move, and the debate has shifted from “is it growing?” to whether order conversion, customer mix, and margins can hold at the same time.

2. Four Things That Matter

Focus 1: Can the $16 billion AI semiconductor guide be delivered?

Q2 AI semiconductor revenue already reached $10.8 billion (+143% YoY), with bookings of more than $30 billion—well ahead of shipments. The Q3 guide requires another step-up. The test is whether custom accelerators (XPU/TPU) and AI networking ramps together. A print at or above $16 billion would reinforce the “second-half acceleration” story. A clear miss would reopen questions on capacity, customer timing, or revenue recognition.

Focus 2: Q4 guidance and the path to $56 billion of full-year AI revenue

Q3 consensus already sits near the company midpoint, so the after-hours reaction is more likely to hinge on the Q4 outlook. Street Q4 revenue is around $34.9 billion. Management has pointed to full-year AI semiconductor revenue of about $56 billion (about +180% YoY) and reiterated fiscal 2027 AI revenue of more than $100 billion. An upward Q4 revision, or a clearer gigawatt delivery cadence, is what the market needs to digest elevated expectations. An in-line guide may be read as visibility peaking.

Focus 3: Google TPU share versus customer diversification

Google remains the largest customer, and the stock keeps trading rumors of in-house / MediaTek share shift. Street base case is that Broadcom’s multi-generation TPU work with Google is still the plan of record, while Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and others support a fiscal 2027 shipment outlook of about 10 GW. The tell is not another design-win headline. It is funded capacity, site readiness, and purchase-order conversion. Lower customer concentration is what would move the valuation from a “single-customer premium” to a “platform premium.”

Focus 4: Mix-driven margins and cash flow

A higher AI hardware mix pressures gross margin. The company expects Q3 non-GAAP operating margin of about 67% and adjusted EBITDA of about 68% of revenue, with gross margin likely easing from about 77% in Q2 to about 74%. Q2 free cash flow was about $10.26 billion, or about 46% of revenue; software remains the profit and cash-flow ballast. If margins fall faster than guided and software growth does not offset it, the market may re-label “high growth” as “lower quality.”

3. Upside and Downside

Upside catalysts:

  • AI semiconductor revenue at or above $16 billion, with networking holding its share—confirmation of a compute-plus-interconnect flywheel.
  • Q4 revenue guidance clearly above the roughly $34.9 billion consensus, plus more specific 2027 delivery and order-conversion detail.
  • Management addresses Google share concerns and shows other top-tier customers ramping, easing the concentration narrative.

Downside risks:

  • Results only meet the midpoint and Q4 commentary is cautious, inviting profit-taking after a high-expectation setup.
  • Gross margin or operating margin slips below the roughly 67%–68% band, raising fears that a rising ASIC mix is eroding earnings quality.
  • Large-customer timing noise, competitors entering custom silicon, or financing/leverage headlines weighing on risk appetite.

4. Trading Framework

Bull case: AI revenue is delivered with a constructive Q4 outlook, customer mix improves, and margins stay on guide. That combination could support a valuation repair from the pullback. The long beat streak still makes “beat and raise” the strongest setup.

Bear case: Numbers are merely in line, margins compress more than expected, or management ducks share and conversion detail. That can trigger the two-way move already priced in options, especially if high growth is already in the stock.

Key numbers:

  • Total revenue and YoY growth
  • Whether AI semiconductor revenue reaches about $16 billion
  • Q4 revenue and margin guidance
  • Gross margin, operating margin, and free cash flow

Tactical notes:

  • Into the print: Price is hugging the 200-day moving average; risk/reward is only average. Keep event risk light. Avoid adding leveraged longs below 368.
  • Long setup: A close back above 379–385, with pullbacks holding 368. Upside references 391 / 400. Stops can sit at 365, or below 350 depending on risk tolerance.
  • Short / hedge setup: A gap that cannot reclaim 368, or a failed push through 377–385. Downside references 356 / 350 / 340.

1. Apple CEO handover is live · Sept. 9 event now in the countdown
John Ternus officially takes over as CEO today; Tim Cook becomes executive chairman and will still handle White House and China supply-chain relations. His first public test is only eight days away: the Sept. 9 product event, where the market is watching a first foldable iPhone, a rebuilt Siri on a Gemini foundation, and on-device AI hardware. A hardware-engineer CEO reframes the Apple trade from a replacement cycle into an AI-device validation window.
🎯 Beneficiaries: AAPL, MU, TSM; Key catalyst: Sept. 9 event pricing and supply-chain confirmation; pre-market will be highly sensitive to foldable/Siri details.

2. Nvidia puts $3.5B into MediaTek · NVLink Fusion opens the rack
NVIDIA said it will buy $3.5 billion of MediaTek convertible bonds and pull MediaTek onto NVLink Fusion, so customers can plug custom XPUs straight into Nvidia rack-scale AI factories. The pact covers cloud AI infrastructure, RTX/DGX Spark local compute, and auto platforms; Alphabet also joined the convertible deal. The read-through: custom silicon is being re-routed through Nvidia’s interconnect and rack stack, not around it.
🎯 Beneficiaries: NVDA, TSM, AVGO; Key catalyst: whether custom chips still need the NVLink rack; watch after-hours pricing of the “circular financing” debate.

3. Intel gets another White House nod · government-as-shareholder narrative heats up
INTC firmed in pre-market after President Trump said he had a “great meeting” with CEO Lip-Bu Tan. Washington last year converted CHIPS grants into an equity stake of about 10%, making the U.S. government one of Intel’s largest shareholders. The tape is trading 18A / onshore foundry optionality plus the chance of a large external customer, against a backdrop of tight TSMC capacity.
🎯 Beneficiaries: INTC, AMKR, TSM; Key catalyst: further White House comments and government-stake headlines; short-term follow-through depends on volume.

4.Tesla rips higher against a weak tape · Optimus + data-center power
Major indexes slipped Monday on oil and rate-hike odds; TSLA still gained about 5%. Over the weekend Elon Musk said Tesla and SpaceX are each building 100 GW a year of solar capacity as fast as possible, and that in-house turbine-blade casting at SpaceX could pull natural-gas turbines online by up to 18 months — a direct hit on the AI data-center power bottleneck. Optimus has also started production at Fremont, with early units headed into Tesla’s own factories for a closed-loop training cycle.
🎯 Beneficiaries: TSLA, VST; Key catalyst: robot production progress plus energy-buildout proof, as a hedge against weaker auto economics.

5.Meta locks in up to 6.6 GW of nuclear · AI power turns from theme into contracts
Meta said it struck deals with Oklo, Vistra and TerraPower for up to 6.6 GW of nuclear supply by 2035 for data centers in the PJM region, on top of its earlier long-term deal with Constellation. AI capex is migrating from GPUs to “power and plants”; nuclear and independent power producers are now in the order-verification layer.
🎯 Beneficiaries: META, OKLO, VST, CEG; Key catalyst: hyperscaler power PPAs hitting the tape; watch nuclear-name volume and follow-on flows.

Trading note: Growth is being pulled two ways — Apple’s CEO handover, Nvidia’s ecosystem lock-in, and robot/nuclear orders on the bid; renewed U.S.–Iran strikes lifting oil and ~60% odds of a September hike on the offer. Flows are paying for verifiable orders and policy backing. Size risk with volume and VIX; don’t chase rich chip multiples into an oil spike.
U.S. equities have been more volatile lately. This is for information only and is not investment advice.

I. Hot News Highlights

Federal Reserve Dynamics

September Hike Pricing Stays Elevated; ISM and Payrolls Are This Week’s Tests

  • After Warsh’s Jackson Hole speech, markets still price about a 58% chance of a 25 bp September hike.
  • Two-year Treasury yields remain high, and front-end rates continue to pressure growth stocks and precious metals.
  • Attention turns to August ISM manufacturing (consensus about 55.2) and Friday’s payrolls, which will determine whether hike odds can move higher still.
    Market Impact: The rate path plus higher oil is reviving sticky-inflation concerns. If ISM and jobs soften, hike pricing could still fade.

International Commodities

Trump Signals Possible Broader Strikes on Iran; Oil Rises Sharply

  • U.S. forces struck two missile launchers on Larak Island over the weekend, saying Iran was preparing to fire mine-equipped rockets into the Strait of Hormuz; Tehran later claimed retaliation.
  • Trump said potential strikes could escalate and posted Kharg Island-related imagery on social media; Reuters said the U.S. had not confirmed a strike on that oil-export hub.
  • Brent moved back above $90 and WTI recovered to around $85, a clear rebound from Friday’s lows.
    Market Impact: Strait transit and export-facility security are again the core of oil pricing. Higher crude reinforces the inflation–hike loop, and energy stocks are relatively resilient.

Macroeconomic Policy

Secondary Sanctions Run Alongside the SPR Narrative

  • Treasury is still adding Iran secondary sanctions on a weekly cadence, focused on banks, shipping and digital-asset channels.
  • Trump had said Venezuelan oil would refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve, but the White House has not released verifiable details.
  • Canadian retaliatory tariffs remain scheduled for September 8.
    Market Impact: Policy signaling is hawkish, but near-term oil is still driven by battlefield headlines. Trade and sanctions spillover could disturb dollar-liquidity expectations.

II. Market Review

Commodities & Forex Performance

  • Spot Gold: Approx. $4,459/oz, +0.23%
  • Spot Silver: Approx. $66.8/oz, +0.47%
  • WTI Crude: Approx. $86.6/bbl, +1.04%
  • Brent Crude: Approx. $88.87/bbl, +0.57%
  • US Dollar Index (DXY): Approx. 99.4, -0.01%

Driver Analysis: Renewed U.S.–Iran clashes and Trump’s escalation comments put Hormuz disruption risk back into crude, with Brent reclaiming the $90 area. Gold did not rally in lockstep, showing capital is trading the oil–inflation–hike chain rather than pure safe-haven demand. Institutions see continued divergence: geopolitics supports oil, hawkish rates cap metals. A confirmed strike on export hubs such as Kharg could amplify oil volatility.

Cryptocurrency Performance

  • BTC: Approx. $78,750, +1.04%
  • ETH: Approx. $2,473, +1.9%
  • Crypto Total Market Cap: Approx. $2.74 trillion, +2.1%
  • Market Liquidations: 24-hour liquidations $158 million, of which shorts $110 million
  • Bitget BTC/USDT Liquidation Map: BTC around $78,700. Heavy short-liquidation clusters sit in the $79,500–$80,000 zone; a break of $80,000 could trigger a further short squeeze. Long-liquidation pressure is concentrated near $77,500–$78,000; a break of $78,000 could accelerate leveraged-long liquidations and keep short-term volatility elevated.

  • Spot ETF Net Flows: August 28 net outflow about $202 million, ending a nine-session inflow streak; Monday’s complete print is still pending.

Driver Analysis: Lower equities, higher oil and still-elevated hike odds are a headwind for risk assets, but Bitcoin remains more resilient than gold and equity indexes and still posted about a 23% August gain. ETH is firmer on the day, though the broader tape still favors hard-asset exposure over high-beta alts. Institutional consensus is that geopolitics and rates jointly set the near-term tone, with $80,000 the bull-bear dividing line.

US Equity Index Performance

  • Dow Jones: Closed at 53,196.54, -0.68%
  • S&P 500: Closed around 7,677, -0.45%
  • Nasdaq: Closed around 26,310, down about 0.35%, with energy and Tesla partly offsetting tech weakness

August still finished higher: the Dow gained about 1.4% on the month, the S&P about 2.4% and the Nasdaq about 3.5%.

Tech Giants Dynamics

  • NVDA: $219.40, +0.85%
  • AAPL: $315.40, -1.35%
  • MSFT: $510.90, -0.51%
  • GOOGL: $338.00, -2.48%
  • AMZN: $260.90, -2.08%
  • META: $571.70, -1.09%
  • TSLA: $365.90, +4.91%

Performance Summary & Driver Analysis: Monday’s decline was uneven. Alphabet was the main index drag and Amazon gave back Friday’s cloud-logic gains. Nvidia stabilized after Friday’s drop, suggesting selling pressure eased. Tesla jumped nearly 5% and became the Nasdaq’s most important offset, as investors traded its energy and grid narrative. The overlay remains “geopolitics plus rates” compressing growth multiples; single-stock outcomes still depend on independent catalysts.

Sector Movers Observation

Energy – Stronger

  • Representative stocks: Exxon Mobil up about 2%; large oil names generally followed crude higher.
  • Drivers: The Larak Island exchange of fire and broader-strike expectations lifted the supply-disruption premium.

EVs / Energy Tech – Counter-Trend Rally

  • Representative stocks: Tesla up nearly 5%.
  • Drivers: The solar and grid-self-sufficiency narrative plus a bounce from oversold levels, as capital looked for elasticity outside the hike trade.

Mega-Cap Tech / Internet – Pullback

  • Representative stocks: Alphabet down more than 2%; Amazon down more than 2%; Apple down more than 1%.
  • Drivers: Higher oil reinforced hike pricing, long-duration growth was pressured, and Friday’s cloud premium was partly cashed in.

III. In-Depth US Equity Analysis

1. Tesla (TSLA) – Rises Nearly 5% Against the Tape

Event Overview: Tesla closed up about 4.9% at $365.90, the clearest offset among the three major indexes. Musk had confirmed that SpaceX and Tesla are accelerating 100 GW of annual solar capacity and moving to cast gas-turbine core parts in-house to shorten power-up timelines.
Market Interpretation: Institutions see an “energy autonomy plus oversold repair” trade rather than a sudden delivery inflection. With oil rising and grid constraints becoming an AI bottleneck, Tesla’s generation and storage narrative is being re-priced. Analysts caution that near-term beta is high and capacity and margins still need proof.
Investment Implications: Suitable as high-beta energy-tech exposure, but position size must match the volatility.

2. Alphabet (GOOGL) – Main Index Drag

Event Overview: Alphabet fell about 2.5% and was a major contributor to the S&P and Nasdaq decline. It had strengthened Friday on the cloud-inference-share thesis and faded with risk appetite on Monday.
Market Interpretation: Institutions treat this as a systemic discount on rate-sensitive growth, not a repudiation of cloud. Barclays’ “model profits flow to the cloud majors” logic still stands, but higher oil and hike odds hit high-multiple internet first.
Investment Implications: Medium term still rests on cloud and ads; near term follows real rates.

3. Nvidia (NVDA) – Stabilizes After the Slide

Event Overview: Nvidia rose about 0.85% to $219.40, ending Friday’s 4.57% giveback. The company had just guided to about 70% FY2028 revenue growth.
Market Interpretation: Institutions view it as a technical repair after a crowded unwind, not a change in the demand thesis. Hike odds still cap multiple expansion; the next catalyst remains supply and customer capex.
Investment Implications: The medium-term demand narrative is intact; avoid chasing already-realized elasticity in the short term.

4. Amazon (AMZN) – Gives Back Cloud-Logic Gains

Event Overview: Amazon fell about 2.1%, reversing part of Friday’s nearly 4% jump. Barclays’ view that AI inference profits accrue to AWS remains in debate.
Market Interpretation: Capital is oscillating between the “cloud toll-booth” thesis and a macro discount. If higher oil keeps lifting hike odds, cloud stocks face duration pressure too, though their fundamental buffer is stronger than pure hardware.
Investment Implications: Watch AWS growth and capex efficiency rather than one-day theme trades.

Key Takeaways

Marvell Technology reported FY2027 Q2 results (quarter ended August 1, 2026) with revenue of $2.739 billion, up about 36.5%–37% year over year and 13% sequentially. That was $39 million above the midpoint of the guidance issued on May 27, 2026, and slightly above Street estimates of about $2.71–$2.72 billion. Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $0.94, up 40% from $0.67 a year earlier and a touch above estimates of about $0.92–$0.93. GAAP net income was $308.0 million, or $0.33 per diluted share. Data center revenue was $2.172 billion, up 46% year over year and 18% sequentially, and accounted for 79% of total sales. Non-GAAP gross margin was 58.9%, down 0.5 percentage point from a year earlier.

Management raised its FY2027 revenue outlook to about $12 billion (roughly +45% year over year, from about $11.5 billion previously) and its FY2028 revenue outlook to about $18 billion (roughly +50%, from about $16.5 billion previously). Data center revenue is expected to grow about 60% in FY2028. Q3 guidance midpoint is $3.15 billion (±5%) for revenue and $1.10 (±$0.05) for non-GAAP EPS, both above then-prevailing Wall Street estimates. Despite the beats and raises, the stock fell as much as about 7.8% after hours to around $222.62. The market’s focus shifted to timing: custom silicon ramps in the second half, and the larger Google-related contribution is framed more as an FY2029-and-beyond story.

  • Murphy said the agreement and other new programs increase management’s confidence that custom silicon revenue will be “meaningfully larger” in FY2029 and the years after. More long-term detail is slated for Investor Day on October 6, 2026.

  • Communications and other revenue $567.8 million, +10% year over year and -3% sequentially, or 21% of sales (26% a year earlier).

  • Management highlighted CXL memory expansion as increasingly important for AI inference deployments; Marvell said it has won additional designs as customers reshape memory architectures amid tight memory supply.

  • Operating cash flow was $605.5 million in the quarter; $200 million was returned via buybacks and about $53.9 million via dividends.

  • FY2027 revenue outlook raised to about $12 billion (~+45% YoY) from about $11.5 billion.
  • FY2028 revenue outlook raised to about $18 billion (~+50% YoY) from about $16.5 billion; data center is expected to grow about 60%.
  • Custom silicon: acceleration from 2H FY2027, more than double in FY2028; the expanded hyperscaler agreement is framed as adding more scale from FY2029 onward.
  • Investor Day: October 6, 2026, in New York, focused on the long-term AI infrastructure strategy.

5. Next-Quarter Guidance (FY2027 Q3, quarter ending October 31, 2026)

  • Revenue $3.150 billion ±5%, implying about +15% sequentially and about +50% year over year at the midpoint; above then-consensus of about $3.00–$3.04 billion.
  • Non-GAAP EPS $1.10 ±$0.05; GAAP EPS $0.53 ±$0.05.
  • GAAP gross margin 52.9%–53.9%; non-GAAP gross margin 57.5%–58.5%, midpoint below Q2’s 58.9%.
  • GAAP operating expenses about $1.015 billion; non-GAAP operating expenses about $655 million.

6. Market Backdrop and Investor Concerns

  • The core tension is not whether the quarter beat, but that the beat was modest and the raise still looks distant. The stock had nearly tripled year to date on the AI trade; investors wanted custom silicon in the near-term numbers, not another two-to-six-quarter wait.
  • After-hours drop of about 7.8%: a small Q2 beat, year-over-year margin compression, and a lower Q3 margin guide offset the revenue and multi-year raises.
  • The Google-related agreement has been described in coverage as a potential ~$120 billion opportunity through FY2033, with equity ownership of up to about $12.2 billion. Management, however, pointed to a meaningfully larger custom-silicon scale in FY2029 and beyond, which the market read as “too far out to re-rate the stock today.”
  • Growth remains tightly tied to data center (already 79% of sales). Connectivity is more visible now; custom is the narrative but lags in reported revenue. Communications and other declined sequentially and cannot offset the timing gap.
  • Earnings quality: the GAAP/non-GAAP gap is wide ($0.94 non-GAAP EPS vs. $0.33 GAAP), driven mainly by stock-based compensation and amortization of acquired intangibles. The stock trades on non-GAAP, but those costs persist.
  • October 6 Investor Day is the next checkpoint. Unless management pulls the custom ramp, Google recognition timing, and margin path closer and more specific, multiple compression can linger.

One-line conclusion: This is a “beat-and-raise on paper, but custom and the Google scale-up still sit further out” print. Near-term price action hinges on whether investors prize the $12B / $18B raises more than the wait for custom silicon to show up in the run-rate.

Nvidia once again shook the market with its better-than-expected performance and released a forward-looking outlook that forced Wall Street to reprice the company.

In its latest earnings call, the company indicated that revenue for the fiscal year ending in January 2028 could increase by more than 70%, far exceeding the prior FactSet consensus expectation of around 45%. TD Cowen analyst Joshua Buchalter called this guidance a "significant potential catalyst for the share price," directly driving Nvidia's stock up 8.7% on Thursday—the largest single-day gain since May 2024. At the close of trading, Nvidia’s market cap reached $5.49 trillion, with a single-day value increase of $441.5 billion, marking the company's second largest single-day market cap boost in history.

Even more striking, some analysts are looking further ahead. Raymond James analyst Simon Leopold wrote in a research note that it "seems possible" for Nvidia to reach $1 trillion in revenue in the fiscal year ending January 2029, while FactSet’s consensus as of Wednesday put that year’s revenue at less than $750 billion.

70% Growth Guidance: Conservative Forecasting Under Supply Constraints

Nvidia’s management made it clear during the earnings call that the 70% growth forecast already factors in supply tightness; without those bottlenecks, the actual number would be higher. JP Morgan also pointed out that despite the guidance being far above expectations, it is likely still conservative. The company explicitly described the current phase as being in a "supply-constrained" state, and if supply were unconstrained, actual demand would be significantly higher.

Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider believes that if Nvidia continues to partner with tech companies to build data centers and further narrow the gap between customer demand and supply, the company could outperform its guidance for the 2028 fiscal year.

On gross margin, Nvidia expects some compression for the remainder of the current fiscal year, but forecasts that next fiscal year margins will remain stable in the 72% to 73% range. Simon Leopold sees this as below recent highs but sufficient to alleviate market pessimism; he notes that, considering higher memory chip prices and intensifying competition from custom chips, this guidance range is "better than the worst-case scenario."

Rubin Platform and Ecosystem Moat: Multiple Growth Engines Take Shape

Buchalter interprets the guidance as a "strong signal of confidence in their business visibility," set against the backdrop of the new-generation chip platform Vera Rubin starting mass production and shipments. Vera Rubin is Nvidia’s next-generation AI chip platform following Blackwell.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon says Nvidia's July quarter results "should remind investors why they own this stock." In his note, he highlighted that demand is accelerating, coinciding with the Rubin platform being Nvidia’s “largest upcoming product cycle in history.”

Rasgon also emphasized that Nvidia's balance sheet is becoming "as important a moat as its technology." The company not only locks in customers for products worth hundreds of billions of dollars through equity investments and revenue-sharing agreements, but can also "support and expand the ecosystem surrounding its products."

Simon Leopold believes that, in terms of revenue, Vera Rubin chips are expected to contribute around 20% of data center revenue in the third fiscal quarter. During the same period, Groq 3 LPX reached full production, with large-scale shipments beginning later this quarter, and new cloud service provider Nebius being an early adopter. The scaling-up pace of Rubin and LPU production both exceeded previous model forecasts, and related estimates have been raised accordingly.

Simon Leopold further noted that Nvidia's progress in its CPU business also exceeded expectations. The Grace CPU’s rolling 12-month revenue has surpassed $5 billion, and the next-generation Vera CPU is already in full production. Based on orders, Nvidia's CPU business has reached an annualized revenue scale of $20 billion, and as supply continues to improve, CPU revenue is expected to more than double in the fiscal year 2028.

Wall Street Remains Divided, But Bulls Accumulate More Chips

Despite Nvidia's strong results boosting bullish confidence, there is still no full market consensus. Buchalter admits that Nvidia’s strategy of providing financing support for its ecosystem partners is "unlikely to convince the bears," but he himself holds a "constructive" view on the sustainability of diversified AI infrastructure spending and Nvidia’s status as the "core enabler."

Overall, Buchalter says bulls have "gained more net points" from these results and bluntly states Nvidia’s stock is "significantly undervalued." Goldman’s Schneider adds that this outlook "may ease investor concerns about high capital expenditure costs."

Analysts expect Nvidia’s revenue to reach $403.5 billion this fiscal year. From this year’s figure to the $1 trillion target, whether Nvidia can turn supply constraints into growth opportunities will be the key variable determining if this expectation can be met.

1. Investment Snapshot

Marvell reports this quarter’s results after the U.S. close on August 27, 2026. Buy-side expects revenue up about 15% sequentially (about +39.0% YoY), with next-quarter guidance around 12% QoQ — a bit above sell-side consensus. The bar is not that high. About half of surveyed funds do not expect a net new chip program this quarter. Single-quarter implied volatility is about 8.8%, well above NVIDIA. The stock has been out of favor for a long time, but the last five months — NVLink Fusion plus the full custom TPU deal with Google — have changed the fundamental backdrop. The real question this time is whether management can turn those partnerships into a verifiable revenue timeline.

2. Four Things to Watch

Focus 1: Why the market still won’t price it in early
Custom-chip revenue is tightly tied to large-customer project timing. There is a track record of splashy framework deals that fail to show up in quarterly numbers, so funds habitually discount partnership headlines. Versus Broadcom, Marvell lacks a comparable multi-customer ramp record. FY2028 forward P/E is about 35x — well above the teens for the sector — and the valuation is widely seen as having already run ahead of the story. Some active money previously rode passive inflows from index inclusion, then cut after the rebound. Positioning is light and expectations are low.

Focus 2: Has the NVIDIA ecosystem slot moved from narrative to orders?
At the end of March, NVIDIA brought Marvell into its AI ecosystem via NVLink Fusion: custom XPUs, NVLink-compatible scale-up networking, plus a silicon-photonics collaboration. NVIDIA also invested about $2 billion. That puts Marvell on the general-purpose GPU interconnect chain as well. The call needs to confirm whether related products are already in guidance — or still just ecosystem narrative.

Focus 3: Don’t read the Google deal’s “$120 billion scale” as backlog
The Google agreement disclosed August 19 and signed July 29 covers custom chips across the TPU ecosystem (inference accelerators, memory controllers, NICs, memory interfaces, near-memory compute). Marvell issued Google about 58.97 million warrants at a $206.58 strike, total size about $12.2 billion; full exercise would give Google about 7% ownership. Warrants vest on cumulative purchases: one tranche for every $500 million purchased, 240 tranches in total, corresponding to a $120 billion cumulative purchase scale by FY2033. That number is a vesting cap, not an order book. Institutions estimate the deal implies about $20 billion of business volume. Versus buy-side FY2027 total-revenue expectations of about $12 billion, the upside is large — but it has to be delivered by a ramp schedule.

Focus 4: Qualitative comments will matter more than this quarter’s growth
The numerical bar is not high. What actually prices the stock is three things: when Google revenue starts contributing (warrant vesting starts counting from FY2027 Q3 — that start date is already close); whether commentary on Microsoft Maia and other existing programs turns more constructive; and whether electro-optical interconnect, CXL and other adjacent businesses get quantified into guidance. If management only repeats the framework and gives no cadence, high volatility plus a 35x multiple leaves plenty of downside.

3. Risks and Opportunities

Upside catalysts:

Key Takeaways

NVIDIA reported FY2027 Q2 revenue (quarter ended July 26, 2026) of $96.221 billion, up 106% year over year and 18% quarter over quarter. That beat analyst estimates by more than 4% and came in about $5.2 billion above the midpoint of the company’s prior Q2 guidance of $91.0 billion.

Non-GAAP adjusted EPS was $2.22, up 120% YoY and above the $2.09 consensus by nearly 6%.

Data center revenue was $89.0 billion (official figure $89.023 billion), up 117% YoY and accounting for about 92.5% of total revenue.

The company guided FY2027 Q3 revenue to a midpoint of $108.0 billion (±2%), implying nearly 90% YoY growth and the first quarter above $100 billion. Gross margin guidance midpoint, however, stepped down to 74.0%. Guidance “does not assume any data center compute revenue from China.”

On the earnings call, management guided FY2028 revenue growth of about 70%, well above the roughly 45% analyst expectation, and said Amazon AWS will deploy an additional 2 million GPUs in 2027–2028. After hours the stock initially dropped about 4%, then turned higher after the call and was up nearly 5% at one point. Shares had already risen more than 10% in the month leading into the report.

Detailed Breakdown

1. Overall revenue and profit

  • Revenue: $96.221 billion, +106% YoY, +18% QoQ; highest YoY growth rate since FY2025 Q2.
  • Prior Q2 revenue guidance midpoint was $91.0 billion; actual result exceeded that by about $5.2 billion.
  • Non-GAAP net income: $53.954 billion, +118% YoY, +18% QoQ.
  • Non-GAAP EPS: $2.22 vs. $2.09 expected.
  • Non-GAAP operating income: $63.956 billion, +124% YoY, above the $61.19 billion analyst estimate; operating margin about 66%.
  • GAAP net income: $59.688 billion, +126% YoY.
  • GAAP EPS: $2.46. GAAP exceeded non-GAAP mainly because the quarter included about $7.77 billion of net gains on equity securities (official figure $7.771 billion), which are excluded from non-GAAP profit.
  • GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were both 75.0%, roughly in line with expectations; up about 2.6 and 2.5 percentage points YoY respectively, and essentially flat QoQ.
  • Non-GAAP operating expenses: $8.232 billion, below the $8.32 billion estimate.
  • GAAP operating expenses: $8.408 billion, +55% YoY, +10% QoQ.
  • Operating cash flow for the quarter: $24.077 billion. Working-capital use rose: accounts receivable increased $22.346 billion, inventory $5.784 billion, and prepaid and other assets $5.497 billion.
  • About $26 billion was returned to shareholders in the quarter (buybacks and dividends). Next-quarter cash dividend is $0.25 per share; record date September 10, 2026; payment date October 1, 2026.

2. Data center performance

  • Data center revenue: $89.0 billion (official $89.023 billion), +117% YoY, +18% QoQ, above analyst estimates of roughly $85.8–85.9 billion by nearly 4%.
  • About 92.5% of total company revenue; the business remains tightly tied to the global AI infrastructure buildout.
  • Growth was driven mainly by the Blackwell Ultra infrastructure r Blackwell still accounted for the majority of system shipments.
  • Hyperscale revenue: $48.71 billion, +102% YoY, +13% QoQ, above the $43.55 billion estimate.
  • Compute Networking: $88.3 billion, above the $84.69 billion estimate.
  • ACIE (AI cloud, industrial and enterprise): $40.31 billion, +138% YoY, +25% QoQ, but below the $41.96 billion market estimate. Official explanation: growth came from AI-native customers, enterprises, sovereign customers, and hyperscalers using AI cloud.
  • Data center Hopper product shipments to China were less than 1% of data center revenue in the quarter.
  • CEO Jensen Huang: “AI has reached an inflection point. It is doing useful work. Tokens are becoming productive and profitable. Compute is now revenue.”
  • A year ago, buildout was driven mainly by one AI lab. Today multiple frontier labs are expanding in parallel, the open-source model ecosystem is thriving, and physical AI is starting to go live.
  • The Vera Rubin platform has entered full-scale production. Racks are already running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. Management expects Rubin to account for about 20% of Q3 data center revenue.

3. Other segments

  • Edge Computing revenue: $7.2 billion (official $7.198 billion), +27% YoY, +13% QoQ, above the $6.61 billion estimate. Covers RTX, Windows on-device AI, robotics, autonomous driving, and is core to the “physical AI” narrative, but remains far smaller than data center.
  • By reported segment: Compute Networking $88.299 billion; Graphics $7.922 billion.
  • Structurally, NVIDIA remains highly dependent on data center in the near term. Edge/graphics is growing but is not yet large enough to change the revenue mix.

4. Supply, purchase commitments, and “AI factory” expansion

  • Management stressed that demand is still accelerating, but supply is the bottleneck. CFO Colette Kress said demand continues to accelerate at current scale and customer forecasts point to a doubling of growth next year, but the company is “supply constrained.” Huang said true demand is well above 70%; if supply were unconstrained, growth would be higher. The broader supply chain is tight, with shortages in memory and other critical components.
  • Purchase commitments to suppliers rose to $279 billion from $119 billion last quarter, driven mainly by memory purchases.
  • 10-Q disclosure: supply and capacity commitments of about $279 billion; total future commitments across supply, cloud, data centers, equity investments, and capex of about $366 billion, plus about $36 billion of AI-cloud-related commitments.
  • On the call: the top five hyperscalers’ capex is expected to approach $800 billion in 2026 and about $1.3 trillion in 2027; cloud-industry backlog already exceeds $2 trillion.
  • NVIDIA is shifting from selling individual GPUs to system-level delivery of full racks, networking, CPUs, software, and deployment solutions. Rubin is not a single chip; it is an “AI factory” architecture that includes Vera CPU, Rubin GPU, Spectrum-6 networking, BlueField, security, storage, software toolchain, and the DSX platform.
  • The company is trying to address bottlenecks in power, land, data-center shells, networking, cooling, and long-term financing at the same time. It has formed strategic partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR, aiming to mobilize more than $500 billion of third-party capital for AI infrastructure. It has also locked land, power, and building-shell capacity with SB Energy at the Ohio PORTS-Pike campus.
  • Responding to “circular financing” questions, Kress said frontier labs such as OpenAI “will become the largest technology companies in history,” face a compute-access bottleneck, and that NVIDIA is providing capital support. “We understand the scale of this support… the capital we put in will generate excellent equity returns.”

5. Next-quarter guidance and FY2028 outlook

FY2027 Q3 guidance:

  • Revenue $108.0 billion ±2%, or about $105.8–110.2 billion; YoY growth about 85.6%–93.3%, midpoint about 89.5%.
  • Above Street consensus (Futu source cited ~$105.15 billion; other compilations roughly $104–105 billion). Even the low end of the range would put the company in the $100 billion-per-quarter club.
  • Guidance explicitly “does not assume any data center compute revenue from China.”
  • GAAP and non-GAAP gross margin midpoint both 74.0% ±50 bps, below the ~75% analyst expectation.
  • GAAP opex about $9.2 billion; non-GAAP about $9.0 billion.
  • Full-year FY2027 GAAP and non-GAAP tax rate expected at 16.0%–18.0% (excluding discrete items and major tax-law changes).
  • Sequentially, the $108.0 billion midpoint is up about 12% from Q2’s $96.2 billion, slower than Q2’s 18% sequential growth.
  • Management said Q3 sequential growth will be driven mainly by ACIE within data center; hyperscale growth is expected to re-accelerate in Q4 and FY2028 as Vera Rubin supply ramps.

Longer-term profit and growth path:

  • Gross margin is expected to bottom around 71%–72% in Q4 and stabilize around 72%–73% in FY2028. The company plans to implement price increases starting in the first quarter of the next fiscal year.
  • FY2028 revenue is expected to grow about 70%, well above the roughly 45% analyst expectation. This is a supply-constrained outlook; the supply bottleneck is expected to last at least through the end of FY2028.
  • Expanded AWS partnership: on top of the existing plan for about 1 million GPUs, an additional 2 million GPUs will be deployed in 2027–2028 (covering Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra), along with Vera CPUs (some integrated with Rubin, some standalone).

6. Market context and investor concerns

  • The core issue was not whether the quarter beat sell-side consensus, but whether it cleared the higher bar already priced in by buyers. Shares had already risen more than 10% in the month before the report; the market was trading the size of the beat.
  • The initial after-hours drop of about 4% was triggered by Q3 gross-margin guidance coming in slightly light; revenue guidance beating consensus but not the most bullish range; and China data center compute being excluded from guidance, so any recovery could not be treated as a locked-in upward revision.
  • The stock turned up nearly 5% after the call, driven by the ~70% FY2028 growth guide, the additional 2 million GPUs for AWS, and management’s emphasis that demand is still accelerating and AI has reached a “compute is revenue” inflection.
  • Structural concern: the beat this quarter was driven mainly by hyperscale customers. ACIE came in below expectations, suggesting enterprise, industrial, and some AI-cloud expansion is slower than previously hoped.
  • Margin pressure comes from early Rubin production costs and yields, rising supply-chain costs for HBM / advanced packaging / substrates, and a richer mix of full-rack system deliveries.
  • The balance sheet is expanding quickly: total assets rose from $206.8 billion on January 25, 2026 to $320.3 billion on July 26, 2026. Accounts receivable stood at $63.059 billion and inventory at $31.575 billion; higher working-capital use is already showing up in free cash flow.
  • Ecosystem investments versus the core business remain in focus: nearly $7.8 billion of net equity-securities gains boosted GAAP profit this quarter, while capital support for labs and the ecosystem has been labeled “circular financing” by some in the market. Management denied that characterization and stressed equity returns.
  • China remains uncertain: China Hopper shipments were under 1% of data center revenue this quarter, and forward guidance fully excludes China data center compute revenue.
  • Capital return did not include a more aggressive commitment beyond existing authorizations. The company said it will increase return of excess free cash flow after strategic uses.

The most important change for Tower Semiconductor (TSEM) is that the market is starting to redefine the company. Tower was traditionally viewed as a specialty analog foundry, but  silicon photonics (SiPho) demand driven by AI data centers is now emerging as its strongest growth engine.
Q2 revenue reached $460 million, up 24% year over year. Excluding one-off items, net income rose to $91 million, implying a 20% net margin. More importantly, Tower guided for record Q3 revenue of $520 million, representing 31% year-over-year growth. This suggests that the silicon photonics capacity ramp is already translating into reported financial results.

Silicon Photonics Expands the Growth Runway

Tower’s strongest fundamental support now comes from improving order visibility. The company has signed $1.3 billion of silicon photonics revenue contracts for 2027 and received $290 million in customer prepayments, while capacity reservations for 2028 are even larger.
Following Q2 results, Tower also raised its 2028 target model to $3.6 billion in revenue and $1.2 billion in net income. At the same time, the company continues to expand 300mm capacity in Japan and is working with partners such as OpenLight and IQE on InP-on-Silicon and next-generation high-speed optical interconnect platforms.
As a result, the market is gradually shifting Tower from a traditional specialty-foundry valuation framework toward an AI optical interconnect growth story.

High Growth Still Comes With a High Valuation

As of August 25, TSEM closed at $212.85, around 33% below its June 22 52-week high of $319.94.
Consensus EPS estimates for 2026 and 2027 are roughly $3.57 and $6.20, implying forward P/E multiples of approximately 60x and 34x, respectively. The valuation remains elevated, but earnings growth is also accelerating rapidly.
If the $1.3 billion SiPho contracts are successfully converted into revenue in 2027 and Tower moves closer to its $3.6 billion 2028 revenue target, earnings growth could continue to absorb part of the current valuation premium.
Recent price targets from BofA, Benchmark and Susquehanna have moved above $330, highlighting the sell side’s increasingly bullish view of Tower’s long-term earnings potential.
The main risks are clear: slower-than-expected silicon photonics capacity expansion, relatively high customer concentration, and potential trade or policy restrictions affecting the optical supply chain. With the stock still trading at a premium valuation, any delay in orders or margin disappointment could amplify downside volatility.

Wait for Technical Confirmation After the Pullback

Technically, momentum has cooled significantly. The stock is currently trading below both its 20-day and 50-day moving averages, leaving the near-term trend weak.
The $208–210 area is the first key support zone, followed by $200 if that level breaks. On the upside, $224–230 is the first major resistance area. A stronger breakout would then reopen the path toward $240–250.
At current levels, the better strategy is to wait for stabilization rather than chase the stock while the downtrend remains intact. If TSEM finds support around $200–210, investors could begin watching for a staged entry opportunity. A recovery above $230 accompanied by stronger volume would provide a clearer signal that capital is returning to the silicon photonics growth theme.
A decisive break below $200, however, would argue for tighter risk control, as further valuation compression remains possible.

Earnings Expectations: $2.71 Billion in Revenue, Up 35% Year-over-Year

Marvell Technology's previous official guidance was for revenue of $2.7 billion (±5%) and adjusted EPS of $0.93 (±$0.05). Susquehanna: Price Target Raised to $265, AI Networking Becomes Core Driver

Susquehanna analyst Christopher Rolland raised his price target to $265 from $230 ahead of the earnings report, maintaining a "Positive" rating. In his report to clients, Rolland wrote that he expects improved earnings and guidance, "primarily driven by strong growth in the AI networking business."

Rolland specifically highlighted the growth potential of Marvell’s high-speed optical communications segment Inphi— the company expects Inphi to grow over 70% by 2027, far above previous targets. More notably, Rolland reaffirmed Marvell’s goal of reaching about $10 billion in custom business revenue by fiscal 2029 — which implies another significant acceleration from the estimated $4 billion base in fiscal 2028. He also pointed out that the agreement with Google covers about $120 billion in custom product business, valid through 2033. This partnership could further boost Marvell's custom XPU targets for fiscal 2028 and 2029.

Wall Street Makes Collective Upgrades: From Rosenblatt to Wells Fargo, Highest Price Target Reaches $310

Susquehanna is not the only firm raising its target price ahead of the earnings report.

Rosenblatt Securities analyst Sajal Dogra sharply raised the target price from $240 to $300, maintaining a "Buy" rating. Dogra expects strong Q2 results, with the optical interconnect business expected to achieve over 25% sequential growth. Rosenblatt forecasts Marvell can achieve about $10.50 in EPS by fiscal 2029.

Wells Fargo analyst Aaron Rakers lifted his target price from $240 to $310, maintaining a "Buy" rating. Rakers views the Google custom AI chip deal as a "significant incremental positive," predicting the transaction could boost EPS by about $2 by fiscal 2029, and expects Marvell to deliver about $11 in EPS by FY29.

UBS analyst Timothy Arcuri raised his target price from $300 to $310. Benchmark analyst Cody Acree maintained a "Buy" rating with a target price of $275. Biggest Highlight: Google’s $120 Billion Mega-Deal and Custom Chip Business Expansion

This agreement further solidifies Marvell’s strategic position in the hyperscale custom chip market. Previously, Marvell has been the core partner for Amazon’s Trainium and Microsoft’s Maia custom chips. Marvell CEO Matt Murphy previously stated that the company’s long-term goal is to capture 20% of the entire custom AI chip market.

However, the competitive landscape remains fierce— Broadcom (AVGO.US) is still a key partner for Google's TPU and is Marvell's strongest competitor in the custom AI chip space.

Higher Expectations and Valuation Challenges

Despite strong performance expectations, Marvell Technology’s biggest challenge comes from valuation. After almost 180% price surge this year, MRVL currently trades at about 17x forward price-to-sales and 74x forward price-to-earnings — making it one of the most highly valued companies in the S&P 500.

Rosenblatt pointed out that the Investor Day on October 6th might be a more significant valuation catalyst than this earnings release. The high valuation means any results that miss expectations or whose "beat is not large enough" could trigger a sharp pullback — which also explains the options market pricing for 10.6% implied volatility.

According to Zhitong Finance APP, as the scale of artificial intelligence infrastructure financing continues to grow, the bond market has begun to reassess the potential credit risks assumed by Broadcom (AVGO.US). As Broadcom is providing guarantees or other forms of credit support for several large-scale AI chip financing transactions, both its bond yields and credit default swap (CDS) prices have risen significantly recently, indicating that investors are increasingly wary of the pressure these arrangements may place on the company's balance sheet.

Data shows that since August, the yield on Broadcom’s corporate bond with a 5.15% coupon maturing in 2031 has cumulatively risen by about 14 basis points. At the same time, the company’s five-year credit default swap price has risen about 28 basis points in the same period, outpacing Oracle (ORCL.US) and SpaceX (SPCX.US).

CDS are commonly used by the market to measure corporate credit risk. An increase in its price means investors have to pay a higher cost to hedge Broadcom’s default risk, also reflecting the market’s demand for higher risk compensation.

The rise in credit risk indicators comes as Broadcom is preparing to participate in a much larger AI infrastructure financing plan. According to previous reports, Broadcom is in talks with several financial institutions to raise over $60 billion in debt for an AI chip financing deal, with AI companies such as Anthropic expected to be major beneficiaries. The specific financing structure is still under discussion, but Broadcom may provide a credit guarantee for some of the senior secured debt.

This is not the first time Broadcom has used its own credit strength to support customer purchases of AI chips.

Earlier this year, Broadcom provided most of the credit support for another financing plan of approximately $35 billion. In that deal, investors including Apollo Global Management and Blackstone Group (BX.US) funded the purchase of Broadcom’s custom AI chips, which were then leased to Anthropic for use.

This financing model helps AI companies obtain large volumes of chips needed to build data centers, while leveraging Broadcom’s balance sheet and credit rating to lower financing costs.

Tony Trzcinka, investment-grade bond portfolio manager at Impax Asset Management, believes that the recent rise in Broadcom’s CDS prices is more likely a reflection of market concerns about the company’s own balance sheet risks rather than a sign of investors losing confidence in the overall AI investment boom. He noted that the change may be related to market expectations for Broadcom to provide further financial guarantees in more chip financing deals in the future.

As tech companies invest hundreds of billions of dollars in AI data center construction, similar guarantee and credit support arrangements have increased significantly this year.

In such transactions, chip suppliers like Broadcom or Nvidia (NVDA.US) are in effect allowing customers to leverage their strong balance sheets and creditworthiness, helping them secure more financing and expand chip purchases.

For chip companies, this model can directly stimulate product sales; for AI companies, it can enable rapid acquisition of computing infrastructure without the need to immediately commit all the necessary capital. However, as transaction sizes grow, the hidden potential risks are beginning to attract the attention of bond investors.

One of the market’s main concerns is that some risks may not be directly reflected as corporate debt in the traditional sense. In addition to explicit debt guarantees, the AI infrastructure financing system also contains long-term leasing contracts, chip procurement commitments, equipment residual value guarantees, and other forms of credit support.

Under normal circumstances, these arrangements may not place obvious pressure on chip companies’ cash flow, but if the AI sector were to suffer a sharp downturn, or if customers’ business conditions deteriorate to the point they are unable to fulfill payment obligations, the guarantor companies may be required to honor those commitments.

At that time, companies like Broadcom might have to shoulder potential payment obligations worth billions or even tens of billions of dollars, even as their own earnings are hit by industry downturns.

JPMorgan strategist Tarek Hamid commented on Broadcom’s potential $60 billion financing deal in a report on Monday, suggesting this further deepens market concerns over “hidden leverage” accumulating within the gigantic AI ecosystem. He pointed out that as leasing contracts, procurement commitments, residual value guarantees, and other credit support arrangements multiply, the scale of related potential obligations could reach several trillion dollars in the future.

This also means that the financial risks created by AI infrastructure construction may be far greater than the amount of debt disclosed directly on corporate financial statements.

Overall, the bond market is not currently questioning Broadcom’s growth prospects in its core AI business, but is beginning to reassess the potential financing risks the company shoulders to promote AI chip sales. From the previous nearly $35 billion financing arrangement to the new deal of over $60 billion currently under discussion, Broadcom is increasingly leveraging its own balance sheet to provide credit support for AI customers.

As investments in AI data centers continue to grow, this approach can help Broadcom further boost chip sales, but the recent rise in bond yields and CDS prices also indicates that the credit markets are now demanding higher risk compensation. The extent to which Broadcom ultimately assumes actual guarantee responsibilities for these financing projects and whether those potential obligations will continue to grow will become key focus points for bond investors assessing the company’s credit risk.

As of Monday’s close, Broadcom shares closed down 2.63% at $358.76.

1. Investment Highlights Snapshot

NVIDIA (NVDA.US) is scheduled to report its fiscal 2027 second-quarter results (ended July) after the U.S. market close on August 26, 2026. Wall Street consensus expects revenue of approximately $91.9 billion (nearly doubling year-over-year), while the company’s prior guidance midpoint stands at about $91.0 billion (±2%). Jefferies is more optimistic, forecasting $95 billion in revenue and expecting October-quarter guidance to be raised to around $108 billion (versus consensus of about $103.7 billion). Morgan Stanley is relatively conservative, projecting roughly $91.2 billion, but still sees sequential growth potentially continuing at a scale of about $10 billion. The market has grown accustomed to “beats and raises.” What will truly determine share-price elasticity are three longer-term questions: whether Rubin can smoothly succeed Blackwell, whether AI demand will remain significantly ahead of supply, and the financing and balance-sheet responsibilities NVIDIA must take on to lock in future demand.

2. Four Key Focus Areas

Focus 1: Blackwell Demand Resilience and Data-Center Growth Quality Blackwell remains the near-term growth driver. Microsoft and Amazon cloud businesses showed clearer improvement during the quarter, while long-term compute commitments from OpenAI, SpaceX, and others continue to support confidence in data-center revenue. Even without meaningful contribution from Rubin yet, current growth is already robust, with potentially greater acceleration after the January quarter next year. Markets will closely watch the contribution split between hyperscalers and AI cloud/enterprise customers, as well as whether networking revenue continues to rise as a percentage of the total.

Focus 2: Rubin Ramp Speed and Valuation Narrative Shift Rubin is the most critical keyword for this earnings call. Jefferies believes the ramp could be meaningfully faster than the early Blackwell phase, as Rubin retains the 72-GPU Oberon NVL72 rack form factor and can reuse the liquid-cooling data-center deployment and manufacturing foundation built with GB200 and GB300. The new design also sharply reduces manual cabling and piping; management has previously indicated that compute-tray assembly time could shrink from roughly two hours to five minutes. This points to NVIDIA turning AI chips into a replicable, scalable “AI factory system.” Jefferies expects VR/R200 to account for about 12% of GPU revenue in fiscal 2027 Q3, rising above 40% in Q4, and becoming the dominant contributor in fiscal 2028 Q1. If this timeline materializes, the valuation narrative will shift from “how long can the Blackwell cycle last” to “can Rubin unlock the next higher base of growth.”

Focus 3: Sustainability of AI Demand-Supply Balance The core market debate has moved beyond single-quarter results to whether the 2027–2028 growth curve can continue to be revised higher. Demand remains supported by hyperscalers, sovereign AI, and enterprise customers, but constraints in the supply chain (especially HBM and advanced packaging), power consumption, and power infrastructure—as well as whether customer capital spending truly converts into verifiable revenue—will be key sentiment drivers.

Focus 4: Circular Financing and Balance-Sheet Responsibilities To secure long-term demand, NVIDIA is mobilizing more than $500 billion in third-party capital through independent financing platforms to support AI infrastructure and has provided residual-value guarantees on OpenAI-related projects (up to a $105 billion scale, corresponding to multi-GW capacity and potentially hundreds of billions in revenue). This can unlock incremental demand but also introduces credit risk, utilization uncertainty, and residual-value exposure. Management’s comments on financing structure, risk exposure, and shareholder-return priorities during the call will directly influence market sentiment.

3. Risks and Opportunities Coexist

Upside Catalysts:

  • Revenue significantly exceeds consensus (approaching or surpassing Jefferies’ $95 billion) and strong October-quarter guidance is provided.
  • Management confirms smooth Rubin production and ramp, releasing positive visibility for 2027–2028.
  • Data-center demand and customer commitments are further reinforced, with financing arrangements viewed as cycle-extending rather than risk-elevating.

Downside Risks:

  • Results merely meet or slightly exceed the guidance midpoint without meaningful upward revision to the longer-term outlook, triggering profit-taking amid high valuations.
  • Rubin progress or customer deployment cadence falls short of expectations, hindering the narrative shift.
  • Financing and guarantee details raise concerns about circular financing or balance-sheet burdens, weighing on sentiment.

4. Trading Strategy Suggestions

Bull Case: If revenue and guidance meaningfully beat expectations and management provides strong endorsement of the Rubin succession and demand sustainability, it could reinforce the “higher base growth” narrative and support valuation recovery.

Bear Risk: If data only meets expectations or guidance is cautious, and financing responsibilities are amplified in interpretation, short-term pullbacks could be triggered in a high-volatility tech environment.

Key Metrics to Watch:

  • Total revenue and year-over-year / sequential growth
  • Data-center revenue and customer-mix breakdown
  • Gross margin performance (guidance around 75%)
  • Next-quarter revenue guidance and full-year / medium-term visibility
  • Rubin-related shipment and progress comments

Operational Suggestions: When results and guidance both exceed expectations and the long-term narrative strengthens, consider accumulation opportunities on pullbacks. If data is muted or financing details raise concerns, watch for short-term volatility risk and avoid chasing highs. Position sizing and stop-losses should be adjusted flexibly according to individual risk tolerance.

  • Resistance: $220–222, $225–228, $232–236
  • Support: $212–214, $208–210, $200, $190–195
  • Upside scenario: Break above $220–222 opens path toward $225–230; pullbacks to $215–218 may offer relative entry references
  • Downside scenario: Break below $212–214 could target $208–210, with further focus on the $200 or $190 zones
