Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has personally stepped in to endorse the company's plan to mobilize over $500 billion in AI infrastructure financing in partnership with six major financial institutions. He made it clear that Nvidia's AI factory computing power is becoming an investable asset class, with demand stemming from real business scenarios. Independent institutional investors will conduct due diligence on each project separately, dismissing external doubts of "circular financing."

On August 10, Jensen Huang announced on social platform X that Nvidia had reached agreements with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to jointly establish an independent financing platform, with the aim to mobilize over $500 billion in third-party capital over time to support AI infrastructure construction. He emphasized that the $500 billion refers to the total amount of third-party capital that the above platforms are designed to mobilize, “neither Nvidia’s revenue nor a commitment by a single fund or to a single customer.”

After the announcement, Nvidia’s stock price fell by as much as 3.2%. The price of the 5-year Credit Default Swap (CDS) measuring the company's credit risk rose to 77.215 basis points on Monday, about 5.3 basis points higher than the previous trading day, the largest single-day gain in two weeks. Analysts believe that this reflects the market's growing attention to Nvidia’s potential credit risk amid such massive financing models.

Wallstreetcn article previously reported, quoting sources from the Financial Times, that Nvidia is looking to jointly raise up to $500 billion with Wall Street giants Apollo, Blackstone, BlackRock’s GIP, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR as a consortium for AI infrastructure projects, covering AI chip procurement, power production, and data center construction.

Following related reports, "Dr. Doom" Jim Chanos posted a sarcastic comment on Nvidia’s joint AI infrastructure financing with Blackstone and other financial giants, likening it to the financial engineering of the 2008 financial crisis, and implying that if the AI bubble bursts, the parties involved may repeat the fate of Wall Street executives being questioned by Congress at that time.

AI Factory: From "Buying Chips" to "Financeable Infrastructure"

In his post, Jensen Huang systematically explained the asset logic behind Nvidia’s AI factory, seeking to redefine the market’s perception of this business model.

He stated that the AI industry has moved from the era where enterprises purchased chips project by project and built their own data centers to a new stage where AI factories can be financed as productive infrastructure—with replicable platforms, long-term institutional capital support, and a diversified customer base using computing power to generate revenue.

Jensen Huang emphasized that Nvidia's computing power is not merely chips, but a comprehensive AI factory platform that includes accelerated computing, networking, system software, AI frameworks, and a global developer ecosystem.

He pointed out that a single Nvidia AI factory can simultaneously serve multiple customers and workloads, offering flexibility and interchangeability; when the needs of one customer change, the factory can be used by another customer, another cloud provider, or another operator, "This broad ecosystem gives Nvidia’s computing power a vast potential user market, helping to protect residual value."

Huang characterized the above collaboration as "the beginning of open capital markets for AI infrastructure." He stated, these financial institutions are all leading global infrastructure investors with deep expertise in underwriting long-term productive assets; together, both sides will build a replicable financing platform to support the factories needed for the AI ecosystem.

CUDA Software Continues to Appreciate, A100 Still in Commercial Use Six Years On

Jensen Huang focused on the long-term economic value of Nvidia’s computing assets, supported by concrete data.

He explained that CUDA software continues to enhance the performance, efficiency, and total ownership cost of installed infrastructure, allowing AI factories to deliver more intelligence at lower cost throughout their lifecycle, thereby extending their economic value.

Taking the A100 as an example: Nvidia launched the Ampere-based A100 in 2020, and six years later it remains commercially active in AI training, fine-tuning, inference, and high-performance computing, with clients continuing to sign multi-year capacity deals. "The economic life of A100 is extending toward ten years."

On GPU rental pricing, Huang cited market data showing that the H100 one-year rental price has risen from about $1.70 per GPU hour in October 2025 to about $2.35 in March 2026; median cross-provider on-demand pricing increased from about $2.00 per GPU hour in October 2025 to $2.70 in June 2026. The Blackwell series commands an even greater premium, with B200 cloud prices at about $5.30 to $7.05 per GPU hour.

He believes the above data demonstrates the lasting economic value of Nvidia’s computing power.

Direct Response to "Circular Financing" Doubts

Addressing the market’s main concern over "circular financing," Jensen Huang set up a Q&A section in his article to respond directly.

He said the very design of this financing arrangement is intended to address this concern. Demand comes from leading AI labs, AI-native startups, enterprise customers, cloud providers, and countries building AI services—“the demand is real.” Each capital provider will independently conduct due diligence on every project, evaluating client credentials, demand, utilization, cash flow, and residual value. "Nvidia provides the platform, and investors make independent financing decisions."

Regarding Nvidia’s own risk exposure, Huang revealed that in some cases, Nvidia may provide up to 25% residual value support for a single project, "prudently assessed project-by-project." He emphasized this ratio is “far lower than other computing power financing arrangements” and is supplemental rather than a substitute for independent due diligence.

Jensen Huang concluded by placing the construction of AI factories in a broader historical context. He stated that every industrial revolution has been built on infrastructure—electricity, transportation, communications, and computing—and each phase has relied on external financing. "AI factories are the infrastructure of the intelligent era."

He summarized the business logic of AI as a positive feedback loop: Companies use AI to write software, develop drugs, design products, serve customers, automate operations, and build new services; more computing power brings better AI, better AI leads to more usage, more usage brings more revenue, and more revenue drives further investment into computing power.

"This is the virtuous cycle of the AI industrial revolution."

Jensen Huang stated that through this collaboration, Nvidia and the world's leading financial institutions will jointly provide infrastructure financing for this industrial revolution, making AI factories more accessible to businesses, industries, and nations.

Wallstreetcn article also noted that this cooperation is not Nvidia’s first deep involvement in AI industry chain financing.

Previous reports indicated that Nvidia was in talks to provide up to $25 billion in credit guarantees for OpenAI and was discussing financing $350 billion for OpenAI’s chip procurement plan; last month Nvidia also announced an expanded partnership with South Korea’s SK Group, with total business volume expected to exceed $500 billion. These moves show that Nvidia is gradually transitioning from a chip supplier to the capital mobilization core of the AI infrastructure ecosystem.

"Dr. Doom" Draws Parallels to 2008: Next Congressional Hearing?

Simultaneously with Huang’s post, Wall Street’s famous short seller, also known as “Dr. Doom,” James Chanos, shared a thought-provoking comment on social media. He wrote:

“These guys’ next time sitting at the same table explaining AI financing could well be at a Congressional hearing in 2031…”

Chanos’s implication references the 2008 financial crisis—at the time, executives from major Wall Street financial institutions were forced to attend Congressional hearings due to the systemic risks posed by subprime mortgages, credit default swaps, and CDOs. He compared Nvidia’s joint financing arrangement with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR to those financial engineering operations, suggesting that if the AI infrastructure investment bubble pops in a few years, Jensen Huang and these financial executives may together face Congressional inquiries.

Notably, when someone in the comments below his post asked if the parties involved would face criminal charges, Chanos clarified: “No one said anything about going to jail.”

1. Investment Highlights Overview

Rocket Lab is scheduled to report its second-quarter 2026 results after the U.S. market close on August 10, 2026. Wall Street consensus expects revenue of approximately $231–232 million (+59.8%–60% YoY), within the company’s own guidance range of $225–240 million. Adjusted EPS is expected in the range of -$0.06 to -$0.08, reflecting a meaningful narrowing of losses versus the prior-year period. Investors will focus on Electron launch cadence and success rates, Neutron first-flight timeline, and progress on the roughly $8 billion Iridium Communications acquisition. Recent large defense contract wins combined with broader space-sector sentiment swings make this print a key test of growth durability and valuation support.

2. Four Key Focus Areas

Focus 1: Launch Services — Electron Cadence and Neutron First-Flight Timeline

Launch activity remains the core near-term driver. The market will scrutinize the number of Electron missions flown, success rates, and per-launch contribution margins, while closely tracking Neutron development progress, engine testing, and the expected late-2026 first flight. Recent multi-hundred-million-dollar Space Force awards, including an approximately $397 million contract, and the assignment of a Neutron national-security mission with a 2028 deadline have raised expectations for medium-lift capability. Any upside in launch metrics or a reaffirmation of the Neutron schedule would strengthen visibility into the growth trajectory.

Focus 2: Space Systems Mix and Backlog Resilience

Space Systems (satellite manufacturing and components) typically carry higher gross margins than pure launch services, so its revenue contribution and delivery pace directly influence overall profitability. Backlog stood at a record roughly $2.2 billion at the end of Q1; investors will watch sequential order intake and conversion rates in Q2. Management previously guided Q2 GAAP gross margin to 33%–35%, slightly below Q1 levels due to a higher mix of lower-margin contracts. Confirmation that this is temporary rather than structural will be important for assessing the path to margin expansion.

Focus 3: Iridium Acquisition Progress and Valuation Re-rating Potential

The roughly $8 billion acquisition of Iridium, expected to close in mid-2027, is the most significant medium-term catalyst. It positions Rocket Lab to expand from hardware and launch into communications services and data subscriptions, bringing valuable spectrum and an existing customer base. Attention will center on integration timelines, preliminary commentary on revenue mix and margin implications, and any discussion of technical or commercial synergies (such as bundling launches with communications payloads). Positive integration language could support a shift toward higher, more service-oriented valuation multiples.

Focus 4: Full-Year Growth Sustainability and Guidance Updates

Rocket Lab has delivered successive record revenue quarters. A Q2 result near the midpoint of guidance that sustains approximately 60% year-over-year growth would continue that momentum. Markets will also watch for any update to full-year revenue expectations, the trajectory of adjusted EBITDA losses, and management’s tone on second-half launch and Space Systems delivery. In a high-volatility environment for technology and space stocks, guidance language often carries more weight than the single-quarter print itself.

3. Risks and Opportunities Coexist

Upside Catalysts:

  • Electron launch volume and success rates exceed expectations, or the Neutron first-flight timeline is firmly reaffirmed with additional bookings.
  • Revenue meaningfully beats the consensus midpoint while backlog continues to expand and gross margins outperform guidance.
  • Constructive updates on Iridium integration that outline a clear path to service-model synergies and valuation re-rating.

Downside Risks:

  • Softer-than-expected launch cadence or success rates, or any indication of delay in the Neutron schedule.
  • Results that merely meet the midpoint of guidance without an upward revision to the full-year outlook, or margin pressure that raises questions about earnings quality.
  • Spillover from SpaceX-related sector sentiment (elevated capital intensity and share unlocks) combined with high valuation scrutiny.

4. Trading Strategy Suggestions

Bull Case: Clear beats on revenue and launch metrics, resilient backlog, and constructive commentary on Neutron progress plus Iridium integration would reinforce the “commercial space leader + services transition” narrative and support valuation recovery.

Bear Case: In-line or slightly soft results, signs of growth deceleration, or cautious language around Neutron or the acquisition could trigger profit-taking, particularly given elevated options implied volatility (around the 100% level) and an expected post-earnings move of roughly ±15%.

Key Metrics to Watch:

  • Total revenue and year-over-year growth rate
  • Electron launch count, success rate, and Space Systems revenue mix
  • Backlog change and new contract awards
  • Neutron development updates and any full-year guidance revision
  • Gross margin and adjusted EBITDA performance

Trading Considerations: If results and guidance are constructive, look for pullbacks as potential entry points. If the print is uneventful or guidance is cautious, respect short-term volatility and avoid chasing. Position sizing and stop-loss levels should always reflect individual risk tolerance.

Kioxia's profit forecast has been fully revised upward, but after its share price was halved, JPMorgan believes that genuine valuation recovery will have to wait until the market witnesses that long-term agreements "actually work" in practice.

According to Fast Trading Desk, JPMorgan's latest research report released on August 10 maintained an "Overweight" rating, simultaneously raising its profit forecast but lowering the target price from 155,000 yen (for the end of 2026) to 130,000 yen (for the end of 2027).

Profit upgrade: Pricing stronger than expected, eSSD as the core driver

JPMorgan’s core reason for the current upward adjustment is that recent NAND pricing has beaten expectations.

The specific revisions are as follows (all are operating profit):

  • FY2027: Raised from 741.88 billion yen to 800.21 billion yen, a year-on-year increase of about 9 times

  • FY2028: Raised from 1,056.25 billion yen to 1,124.10 billion yen, a year-on-year increase of about 40%

  • FY2029: Raised from 1,392.60 billion yen to 1,456.23 billion yen, a year-on-year increase of about 30%

There are three specific assumption adjustments behind these changes:

First, the timing for consumer-grade NAND price decline will be postponed—from the previously expected Q3 2027 to Q4 2027—reflecting tighter supply-demand dynamics.

Second, the eSSD (enterprise-grade solid-state drives) average price assumption was raised, mainly due to stronger-than-expected price recovery in Q2 2026. JPMorgan still expects that, as multi-year LTA gradually roll out from 2027, pricing will become more stable (with the company's target of 50% LTA coverage in 2028).

Third, the bit shipment forecast remains largely unchanged.

It is noteworthy that JPMorgan maintains a distinctly bullish view on the eSSD market. Despite some market pessimism that "NAND prices may fall as early as Q4 2026", JPMorgan believes that the continued rise in eSSD penetration will be sufficient to offset weaknesses in the consumer-grade NAND sector. They forecast that the overall eSSD TAM (total addressable market) will exceed 820EB next year, up about 55% year-on-year.

Valuation downgrade: LTA needs to "walk the talk"

The target price cut originates from a re-rating of the valuation multiple.

JPMorgan has reduced the target P/E from approximately 11x (about 0.5 standard deviation above the historical average) to around 9x, returning to the 15-year historical average level for global storage vendors.

The previous premium was given because of expectations that LTA would deliver medium-term earnings stability; but now, JPMorgan thinks that "the market needs to see stable results in the actual numbers before buying in."

The report points out that Kioxia plans to introduce multi-year LTAs as an independent company for the first time from 2027, with the target of reaching 50% LTA coverage by 2028. However, past cases where LTA failed to deliver the expected results have made the market cautious.

JPMorgan clearly states that two key dimensions determine the credibility of LTA: (1) Enforceability, such as the effectiveness of penalty clauses; (2) Its ability to smooth the pricing curve, i.e., whether it can truly reduce price volatility.

"A valuation re-rating will still take time until stable effects are proven in actual results." This is JPMorgan's core view.

Share buybacks: First large-scale buyback in the storage industry

While waiting for LTA validation, Kioxia is sending another signal to the market.

The company announced a share buyback program of up to 800 billion yen as it reported results for Q1 of 2026 (April to June), with the buyback window set from August 3 to October 30.

JPMorgan describes this as the "first large-scale buyback in the storage ecosystem," particularly highlighting the brevity of the buyback window.

In terms of FCF yield, JPMorgan expects FY2026 to FY2028 (based on the share price as of August 7) to be 13%, 27%, and 37%, respectively. The company stated at its June investor day that it will actively return excess free cash flow, primarily via dividends (possibly beginning as soon as the end of FY2026).

JPMorgan currently assumes FCF payout ratios of 10%/30%/50% for FY2026-FY2028, equating to total shareholder return (TSR) of approximately 4%/8%/18%. Should the actual return exceed this assumption, there will be further room for valuation re-rating.

As a reference, both Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix target 50% of accumulated FCF for shareholder returns.

GP series: A medium-term variable for potential supply tightening

JPMorgan also focuses on Kioxia's GP product line—an "ultra-high IOPS" series based on SLC (single-level cell) architecture.

Kioxia's three product line strategies are as follows:

  • CM series (TLC architecture, targeting KV Cache applications)

  • GP series (SLC architecture, targeting HBM supplement/expansion scenarios)

  • LC series (QLC architecture, targeting HDD replacement)

The goal is to increase the eSSD market share from around 10% to 15%.

The GP series aims to achieve 100 million IOPS (input/output operations per second), and the company is planning to sample GP1 (10 million IOPS) to some customers before the end of 2026.

Key supply and demand impact: The "die penalty" (capacity overhead) of SLC architecture is 3 to 4 times that of TLC/QLC. This means that even if the bit contribution from the GP series is limited, its overall consumption of supply is far higher proportionally, and could become a structural factor tightening supply and demand mid-term.

JPMorgan has listed progress in GP series development and customer adoption as important medium-term catalysts.

results.title: Broadcom Q3 Preview: Growth Is Priced In, Conversion Is What Matters — JPMorgan Says AI Is Badly Underestimated and Google TPU Fears Are Overdone
results.content:
1. Investment Snapshot

Broadcom (AVGO.US) will report fiscal third-quarter 2026 results after the U.S. close on September 2, 2026. Management has guided quarterly revenue to about $29.4 billion (+84% YoY), including AI semiconductor revenue of about $16 billion (over +200% YoY). Street consensus is roughly $29.2–$29.5 billion in revenue and adjusted EPS of about $3.22 (+90.5% YoY). Ahead of the print, JPMorgan kept an Overweight rating and a $580 price target, arguing the quarter should come in solid and that Q4 guidance is more likely to set the stock. Shares have pulled back meaningfully from the highs, options imply about an 8% move, and the debate has shifted from “is it growing?” to whether order conversion, customer mix, and margins can hold at the same time.

2. Four Things That Matter

Focus 1: Can the $16 billion AI semiconductor guide be delivered?

Q2 AI semiconductor revenue already reached $10.8 billion (+143% YoY), with bookings of more than $30 billion—well ahead of shipments. The Q3 guide requires another step-up. The test is whether custom accelerators (XPU/TPU) and AI networking ramps together. A print at or above $16 billion would reinforce the “second-half acceleration” story. A clear miss would reopen questions on capacity, customer timing, or revenue recognition.

Focus 2: Q4 guidance and the path to $56 billion of full-year AI revenue

Q3 consensus already sits near the company midpoint, so the after-hours reaction is more likely to hinge on the Q4 outlook. Street Q4 revenue is around $34.9 billion. Management has pointed to full-year AI semiconductor revenue of about $56 billion (about +180% YoY) and reiterated fiscal 2027 AI revenue of more than $100 billion. An upward Q4 revision, or a clearer gigawatt delivery cadence, is what the market needs to digest elevated expectations. An in-line guide may be read as visibility peaking.

Focus 3: Google TPU share versus customer diversification

Google remains the largest customer, and the stock keeps trading rumors of in-house / MediaTek share shift. Street base case is that Broadcom’s multi-generation TPU work with Google is still the plan of record, while Anthropic, OpenAI, Meta and others support a fiscal 2027 shipment outlook of about 10 GW. The tell is not another design-win headline. It is funded capacity, site readiness, and purchase-order conversion. Lower customer concentration is what would move the valuation from a “single-customer premium” to a “platform premium.”

Focus 4: Mix-driven margins and cash flow

A higher AI hardware mix pressures gross margin. The company expects Q3 non-GAAP operating margin of about 67% and adjusted EBITDA of about 68% of revenue, with gross margin likely easing from about 77% in Q2 to about 74%. Q2 free cash flow was about $10.26 billion, or about 46% of revenue; software remains the profit and cash-flow ballast. If margins fall faster than guided and software growth does not offset it, the market may re-label “high growth” as “lower quality.”

3. Upside and Downside

Upside catalysts:

  • AI semiconductor revenue at or above $16 billion, with networking holding its share—confirmation of a compute-plus-interconnect flywheel.
  • Q4 revenue guidance clearly above the roughly $34.9 billion consensus, plus more specific 2027 delivery and order-conversion detail.
  • Management addresses Google share concerns and shows other top-tier customers ramping, easing the concentration narrative.

Downside risks:

  • Results only meet the midpoint and Q4 commentary is cautious, inviting profit-taking after a high-expectation setup.
  • Gross margin or operating margin slips below the roughly 67%–68% band, raising fears that a rising ASIC mix is eroding earnings quality.
  • Large-customer timing noise, competitors entering custom silicon, or financing/leverage headlines weighing on risk appetite.

4. Trading Framework

Bull case: AI revenue is delivered with a constructive Q4 outlook, customer mix improves, and margins stay on guide. That combination could support a valuation repair from the pullback. The long beat streak still makes “beat and raise” the strongest setup.

Bear case: Numbers are merely in line, margins compress more than expected, or management ducks share and conversion detail. That can trigger the two-way move already priced in options, especially if high growth is already in the stock.

Key numbers:

  • Total revenue and YoY growth
  • Whether AI semiconductor revenue reaches about $16 billion
  • Q4 revenue and margin guidance
  • Gross margin, operating margin, and free cash flow

Tactical notes:

  • Into the print: Price is hugging the 200-day moving average; risk/reward is only average. Keep event risk light. Avoid adding leveraged longs below 368.
  • Long setup: A close back above 379–385, with pullbacks holding 368. Upside references 391 / 400. Stops can sit at 365, or below 350 depending on risk tolerance.
  • Short / hedge setup: A gap that cannot reclaim 368, or a failed push through 377–385. Downside references 356 / 350 / 340.

Federal Reserve Dynamics

Warsh Reaffirms Inflation Priority; September Hike Pricing Moves Higher

  • In his Jackson Hole debut, Fed Chair Kevin Warsh offered no explicit rate path, but said that if inflation does not return to 2% “clearly and with sufficient speed,” the Fed would have “more work to do.”
  • The two-year Treasury yield rose about 11 basis points on the day. CME data show the probability of a 25 bp September hike climbing from about 35% to roughly 58%–60%.
  • Former Vice Chair Alan Blinder argued the wording itself amounts to another form of forward guidance. Analysts say September payrolls and CPI will still decide the final pricing.
    Market Impact: Higher front-end rates pressured richly valued growth stocks and precious metals, while the dollar firmed. If subsequent data weaken again, hike pricing could still fade.

International Commodities

U.S.–Iran Fighting Resumes; Hormuz Risk Premium Returns

  • Iran’s Revolutionary Guard said it fired missiles at U.S. bases and accused Washington of bombing facilities on Larak Island, causing casualties. U.S. officials said American forces struck two missile launchers on the island after Iran prepared to fire mine-equipped rockets toward the strait.
  • U.S. Central Command said it had diverted 83 commercial vessels, disabled three and boarded two.
  • Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said the department plans weekly additional secondary sanctions on Iran, starting with banks.
    Market Impact: Weekend clashes interrupted hopes of a diplomatic off-ramp. Oil is again pricing supply-disruption risk, lifting both sticky-inflation concerns and safe-haven demand.

Macroeconomic Policy

Trump Says Venezuelan Oil Will Refill the SPR

  • Trump said the U.S. has reached a deal giving it “majority control” of more than 65 billion barrels of Venezuela’s proven reserves and plans to use the oil to refill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve.
  • The White House has not released formal agreement details, and markets remain cautious on executability.
  • Canadian retaliatory tariffs are still due on September 8, so North American trade friction and the energy-supply narrative are running in parallel.
    Market Impact: If reserve replenishment materializes, it could ease U.S. pump prices over the medium term. Near-term oil, however, is still driven by Hormuz, leaving a gap between policy signaling and battlefield reality.

Investment Implications: Watch cloud growth, AI-revenue disclosure and capex returns rather than short-term rate noise.

Event Overview: Marvell raised guidance and grew revenue and profit, yet the stock still dropped about 10%, becoming the emblem of the semiconductor pullback.
Market Interpretation: Institutions say Nvidia has lifted the bar so high that “good growth that is not spectacular” can trigger a valuation reset. Rising hike odds added duration pressure.
Investment Implications: In high-expectation industries, the slope of guidance and share gains matter more than merely positive year-over-year growth.

results.title: Marvell FY2027 Q2 Highlights: Revenue $2.74B, Up 37% YoY; Full-Year Outlook Raised, Shares Still Drop ~8% After Hours
results.content:
Key Takeaways

Marvell Technology reported FY2027 Q2 results (quarter ended August 1, 2026) with revenue of $2.739 billion, up about 36.5%–37% year over year and 13% sequentially. That was $39 million above the midpoint of the guidance issued on May 27, 2026, and slightly above Street estimates of about $2.71–$2.72 billion. Non-GAAP diluted EPS was $0.94, up 40% from $0.67 a year earlier and a touch above estimates of about $0.92–$0.93. GAAP net income was $308.0 million, or $0.33 per diluted share. Data center revenue was $2.172 billion, up 46% year over year and 18% sequentially, and accounted for 79% of total sales. Non-GAAP gross margin was 58.9%, down 0.5 percentage point from a year earlier.

Management raised its FY2027 revenue outlook to about $12 billion (roughly +45% year over year, from about $11.5 billion previously) and its FY2028 revenue outlook to about $18 billion (roughly +50%, from about $16.5 billion previously). Data center revenue is expected to grow about 60% in FY2028. Q3 guidance midpoint is $3.15 billion (±5%) for revenue and $1.10 (±$0.05) for non-GAAP EPS, both above then-prevailing Wall Street estimates. Despite the beats and raises, the stock fell as much as about 7.8% after hours to around $222.62. The market’s focus shifted to timing: custom silicon ramps in the second half, and the larger Google-related contribution is framed more as an FY2029-and-beyond story.

1. Overall Revenue and Profitability

  • Revenue $2.739 billion, +36.5%–37% year over year, +13% quarter over quarter; a quarterly record and $39 million above the prior Q2 guide midpoint.
  • Non-GAAP diluted EPS $0.94, +40% year over year (from $0.67) and up from $0.80 in Q1.
  • GAAP diluted EPS $0.33; GAAP net income $308.0 million; non-GAAP net income $865.9 million.
  • GAAP gross margin 53.1%; non-GAAP gross margin 58.9% (59.4% a year earlier).
  • GAAP operating income $459.7 million, operating margin 16.8%; non-GAAP operating income $1.003 billion, operating margin 36.6% (+180 bps year over year, +160 bps sequentially).
  • Operating cash flow $605.5 million; capex about $126.7 million, implying free cash flow of roughly $479 million.
  • Cash and cash equivalents $3.933 billion as of August 1, 2026. The company bought back $200 million of stock and paid about $53.9 million in dividends during the quarter.

Core Financial Comparison (Company Figures)

Data center revenue $2.172B $1.833B $1.491B +18% +46%
GAAP gross margin 53.1% — — — —
Non-GAAP gross margin 58.9% — 59.4% — -0.5 pt
GAAP net income $308.0M $34.5M $194.8M Sharp rebound +58%
GAAP diluted EPS $0.33 $0.04 $0.22 — +50%
Non-GAAP net income $865.9M — — — —
Non-GAAP diluted EPS $0.94 $0.80 $0.67 +18% +40%
 
 

2. Data Center Performance

  • Data center revenue $2.172 billion, +46% year over year and +18% sequentially, or 79% of total sales (74% a year earlier; 76% in Q1). That beat the LSEG economist estimate of about $2.13 billion.
  • Chairman and CEO Matt Murphy said growth was broad-based across the data center portfolio: connectivity demand is strong, and the custom business is expected to accelerate significantly beginning in the second half of FY2027.
  • Management expects data center custom silicon to ramp sharply in 2H FY2027 and more than double year over year in FY2028. Growth is expected from XPUs and XPU-adjacent products, including CXL and custom networking.
  • On the call, management confirmed an 8-K disclosure of an expanded commercial agreement and related warrants with a major hyperscaler. Analysts identified the partner as Google. Murphy said the work covers programs already underway, newly won designs, and potential future programs, spanning AI inference accelerators, storage controllers, NICs, memory-interface controllers, and near-memory compute products attached to the TPU ecosystem.
  • Murphy said the agreement and other new programs increase management’s confidence that custom silicon revenue will be “meaningfully larger” in FY2029 and the years after. More long-term detail is slated for Investor Day on October 6, 2026.

3. Other End Markets

  • Communications and other revenue $567.8 million, +10% year over year and -3% sequentially, or 21% of sales (26% a year earlier).
  • This segment is no longer the growth engine and continues to shrink as a share of the mix.
  • Management highlighted CXL memory expansion as increasingly important for AI inference deployments; Marvell said it has won additional designs as customers reshape memory architectures amid tight memory supply.

4. Capital Allocation and Forward Plans

  • Operating cash flow was $605.5 million in the quarter; $200 million was returned via buybacks and about $53.9 million via dividends.
  • Period-end snapshot: total assets $27.555 billion, long-term debt $4.963 billion, stockholders’ equity $18.532 billion.
  • FY2027 revenue outlook raised to about $12 billion (~+45% YoY) from about $11.5 billion.
  • FY2028 revenue outlook raised to about $18 billion (~+50% YoY) from about $16.5 billion; data center is expected to grow about 60%.
  • Custom silicon: acceleration from 2H FY2027, more than double in FY2028; the expanded hyperscaler agreement is framed as adding more scale from FY2029 onward.
  • Investor Day: October 6, 2026, in New York, focused on the long-term AI infrastructure strategy.

5. Next-Quarter Guidance (FY2027 Q3, quarter ending October 31, 2026)

  • Revenue $3.150 billion ±5%, implying about +15% sequentially and about +50% year over year at the midpoint; above then-consensus of about $3.00–$3.04 billion.
  • Non-GAAP EPS $1.10 ±$0.05; GAAP EPS $0.53 ±$0.05.
  • GAAP gross margin 52.9%–53.9%; non-GAAP gross margin 57.5%–58.5%, midpoint below Q2’s 58.9%.
  • GAAP operating expenses about $1.015 billion; non-GAAP operating expenses about $655 million.
  • Basic weighted-average shares about 900 million; diluted about 921 million.

Guidance Comparison

Item Company guide Street (public compilations) What matters
Q3 revenue $3.150B ±5% ~$3.00–$3.04B Midpoint ~4%–5% above consensus
Q3 non-GAAP EPS $1.10 ±$0.05 ~$1.07–$1.08 Modest beat
Q3 non-GAAP GM 57.5%–58.5% — Below Q2’s 58.9%
FY27 revenue ~$12B (+45%) Prior company view ~$11.5B Raise of ~$500M
FY28 revenue ~$18B (+50%) Prior company view ~$16.5B Raise of ~$1.5B
Custom ramp timing Accelerates from 2H FY27 Market wanted more in the near-term guide Limited near-term contribution; main reason for the after-hours selloff
 
 

6. Market Backdrop and Investor Concerns

  • The core tension is not whether the quarter beat, but that the beat was modest and the raise still looks distant. The stock had nearly tripled year to date on the AI trade; investors wanted custom silicon in the near-term numbers, not another two-to-six-quarter wait.
  • After-hours drop of about 7.8%: a small Q2 beat, year-over-year margin compression, and a lower Q3 margin guide offset the revenue and multi-year raises.
  • The Google-related agreement has been described in coverage as a potential ~$120 billion opportunity through FY2033, with equity ownership of up to about $12.2 billion. Management, however, pointed to a meaningfully larger custom-silicon scale in FY2029 and beyond, which the market read as “too far out to re-rate the stock today.”
  • Growth remains tightly tied to data center (already 79% of sales). Connectivity is more visible now; custom is the narrative but lags in reported revenue. Communications and other declined sequentially and cannot offset the timing gap.
  • Earnings quality: the GAAP/non-GAAP gap is wide ($0.94 non-GAAP EPS vs. $0.33 GAAP), driven mainly by stock-based compensation and amortization of acquired intangibles. The stock trades on non-GAAP, but those costs persist.
  • October 6 Investor Day is the next checkpoint. Unless management pulls the custom ramp, Google recognition timing, and margin path closer and more specific, multiple compression can linger.

One-line conclusion: This is a “beat-and-raise on paper, but custom and the Google scale-up still sit further out” print. Near-term price action hinges on whether investors prize the $12B / $18B raises more than the wait for custom silicon to show up in the run-rate.

Disclaimer

This note is for information only and is not investment advice. Figures are drawn from Marvell’s official press release, publicly reported earnings-call remarks, and contemporaneous coverage. Consensus estimates can differ by data vendor. Comments on specific customer programs, custom-silicon doubling, and FY2029 scale are forward-looking and should be read against the company’s SEC filings and official releases.

results.title: NVIDIA ignites a new Wall Street expectation: $1 trillion revenue sprint for FY2028?
results.content:
Nvidia once again shook the market with its better-than-expected performance and released a forward-looking outlook that forced Wall Street to reprice the company.

In its latest earnings call, the company indicated that revenue for the fiscal year ending in January 2028 could increase by more than 70%, far exceeding the prior FactSet consensus expectation of around 45%. TD Cowen analyst Joshua Buchalter called this guidance a "significant potential catalyst for the share price," directly driving Nvidia's stock up 8.7% on Thursday—the largest single-day gain since May 2024. At the close of trading, Nvidia’s market cap reached $5.49 trillion, with a single-day value increase of $441.5 billion, marking the company's second largest single-day market cap boost in history.

Even more striking, some analysts are looking further ahead. Raymond James analyst Simon Leopold wrote in a research note that it "seems possible" for Nvidia to reach $1 trillion in revenue in the fiscal year ending January 2029, while FactSet’s consensus as of Wednesday put that year’s revenue at less than $750 billion.

70% Growth Guidance: Conservative Forecasting Under Supply Constraints

Nvidia’s management made it clear during the earnings call that the 70% growth forecast already factors in supply tightness; without those bottlenecks, the actual number would be higher. JP Morgan also pointed out that despite the guidance being far above expectations, it is likely still conservative. The company explicitly described the current phase as being in a "supply-constrained" state, and if supply were unconstrained, actual demand would be significantly higher.

Goldman Sachs analyst James Schneider believes that if Nvidia continues to partner with tech companies to build data centers and further narrow the gap between customer demand and supply, the company could outperform its guidance for the 2028 fiscal year.

On gross margin, Nvidia expects some compression for the remainder of the current fiscal year, but forecasts that next fiscal year margins will remain stable in the 72% to 73% range. Simon Leopold sees this as below recent highs but sufficient to alleviate market pessimism; he notes that, considering higher memory chip prices and intensifying competition from custom chips, this guidance range is "better than the worst-case scenario."

Rubin Platform and Ecosystem Moat: Multiple Growth Engines Take Shape

Buchalter interprets the guidance as a "strong signal of confidence in their business visibility," set against the backdrop of the new-generation chip platform Vera Rubin starting mass production and shipments. Vera Rubin is Nvidia’s next-generation AI chip platform following Blackwell.

Bernstein analyst Stacy Rasgon says Nvidia's July quarter results "should remind investors why they own this stock." In his note, he highlighted that demand is accelerating, coinciding with the Rubin platform being Nvidia’s “largest upcoming product cycle in history.”

Rasgon also emphasized that Nvidia's balance sheet is becoming "as important a moat as its technology." The company not only locks in customers for products worth hundreds of billions of dollars through equity investments and revenue-sharing agreements, but can also "support and expand the ecosystem surrounding its products."

Simon Leopold believes that, in terms of revenue, Vera Rubin chips are expected to contribute around 20% of data center revenue in the third fiscal quarter. During the same period, Groq 3 LPX reached full production, with large-scale shipments beginning later this quarter, and new cloud service provider Nebius being an early adopter. The scaling-up pace of Rubin and LPU production both exceeded previous model forecasts, and related estimates have been raised accordingly.

Simon Leopold further noted that Nvidia's progress in its CPU business also exceeded expectations. The Grace CPU’s rolling 12-month revenue has surpassed $5 billion, and the next-generation Vera CPU is already in full production. Based on orders, Nvidia's CPU business has reached an annualized revenue scale of $20 billion, and as supply continues to improve, CPU revenue is expected to more than double in the fiscal year 2028.

Wall Street Remains Divided, But Bulls Accumulate More Chips

Despite Nvidia's strong results boosting bullish confidence, there is still no full market consensus. Buchalter admits that Nvidia’s strategy of providing financing support for its ecosystem partners is "unlikely to convince the bears," but he himself holds a "constructive" view on the sustainability of diversified AI infrastructure spending and Nvidia’s status as the "core enabler."

Overall, Buchalter says bulls have "gained more net points" from these results and bluntly states Nvidia’s stock is "significantly undervalued." Goldman’s Schneider adds that this outlook "may ease investor concerns about high capital expenditure costs."

Analysts expect Nvidia’s revenue to reach $403.5 billion this fiscal year. From this year’s figure to the $1 trillion target, whether Nvidia can turn supply constraints into growth opportunities will be the key variable determining if this expectation can be met.

results.title: Bitget UEX Daily | Warsh’s Jackson Hole Debut Tonight; Nvidia Surges Nearly 9% and Breaks the “Earnings-Day Curse”; Spot Bitcoin ETFs See $2.8 Billion of Inflows Over Eight Sessions (August 28, 2026)
results.content:
I. Hot News Highlights

Federal Reserve Dynamics

Warsh’s Jackson Hole Debut Tonight; Markets Focus on Inflation Credibility

  • Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will deliver his first Jackson Hole keynote at 22:00 Friday (UTC+8). The core watchpoints are his commitment to the inflation target, his communication framework, and the Fed’s role in a high-debt environment.
  • Goldman Sachs expects no explicit guidance on the September meeting. He is more likely to reaffirm the 2% target, explain a “say less and let markets react to data” communication approach, and discuss productivity and global shocks.
  • CME data put the probability of holding rates unchanged in September at about 63.5%, versus about 36.5% for a cumulative 25 bp hike.
    Market Impact: The speech is the week’s pricing anchor. If he again avoids a roadmap, long-end yields and the dollar could become more volatile; if he restates a hard anti-inflation stance, rate-sensitive growth stocks may face near-term pressure.

International Commodities

U.S. Declines to Return to the June Iran Understanding; Hormuz Stalemate Continues

  • The Wall Street Journal, citing people familiar with the matter, reported that the Trump administration has repeatedly told mediators it has no intention of returning to the June memorandum of understanding with Iran.
  • Iranian officials said they have prepared a list of conditions for Washington. Ships are currently allowed only through a temporary designated channel, and future passage would depend on a new understanding.
  • Bloomberg reported that Venezuela is assessing a possible exit from OPEC, a topic already raised in talks with U.S. officials.
    Market Impact: Expectations of a diplomatic breakthrough have cooled, giving oil geopolitical support. Concerns about OPEC cohesion have risen, increasing near-term crude volatility and making the sticky-inflation narrative harder to fade.

Macroeconomic Policy

Canada Widens Retaliatory Tariffs; Data-Center Constraints Persist

  • Canada added copper wire, charcoal and other items to its 50% retaliatory-tariff list. Coverage remains calibrated to about $20 billion of U.S. goods, with measures effective September 8.
  • Institutions continue to warn that planned data centers face delay or cancellation risk, as power and community constraints slow AI infrastructure delivery.
    Market Impact: North American trade friction and power bottlenecks form a dual constraint. Domestic equipment and supply-chain themes are drawing attention, and tech capex expectations are becoming more differentiated.

II. Market Review

Commodities Forex Performance

Gold consolidated at elevated levels ahead of Warsh’s speech, while silver received support from industrial demand. Dollar-call hedging in the options market increased, showing traders are reluctant to accumulate large USD shorts before the speech. Institutional views hold that near-term commodities are driven by a “geopolitical stalemate + policy-communication vacuum,” with the linkage running from fading negotiation hopes → oil support → persistent sticky-inflation concerns → metals and FX waiting for Warsh to set the tone.

The equal-weight SP did not keep pace, and gains were highly concentrated in Nvidia and software earnings winners. Nvidia’s single-day market-cap gain of about $440 billion explained most of the index advance. Apple and Microsoft were relatively steady, while Amazon and Alphabet lagged on valuation digestion and rotation. The software rebound suggests investors are no longer indiscriminately pricing a “SaaS winter,” but are again differentiating names that can convert AI into recurring revenue.

Sector Movers Observation

Software / SaaS – Sharp Rebound

Markets also focused on reports that Nvidia is expanding its AI-ecosystem investments.

Giving high-growth guidance a full year early is rare and implies improved order visibility; the “supply-constrained” qualifier also means bottlenecks remain and the pricing logic is not over. Analysts caution that index gains were overly concentrated in one mega-cap weight and that follow-through across the broader AI chain still needs confirmation.
Investment Implications: The medium-term demand thesis is stronger after the beat, but near-term crowding has increased. Monitor supply release and divergence in customer capex.

2. Salesforce (CRM) – Beat and Raised Full-Year Guidance

Event Overview: Salesforce reported FY2027 Q2 revenue of $11.3 billion, up 11%, and subscription-and-support revenue of $10.8 billion. Current remaining performance obligation rose 14% year-over-year to $33.5 billion. Full-year revenue guidance was raised to $46.1–$46.4 billion, implying 11%–12% growth. The company also announced Claudeforce, a partnership with Anthropic. Shares jumped more than 22%.
Market Interpretation: Institutions view the move as a correction of the “software growth stall” pricing. Accelerating cRPO and a guidance raise suggest AI features are entering renewal and expansion cycles rather than remaining conceptual. Analysts will watch the split between Informatica’s contribution and organic growth, as well as the margin impact of pending acquisitions.
Investment Implications: The key variable for software repair is recurring-revenue quality, not one-off thematic trading.

3. CrowdStrike (CRWD) – Record Net-New ARR

Event Overview: CrowdStrike reported FY2027 Q2 revenue of $1.47 billion, up 26%, and non-GAAP EPS of $0.31. Ending ARR reached $5.84 billion, with record net-new ARR of $333 million, up 51% year-over-year. ARR from Falcon Flex accounts doubled to $2.29 billion. The company raised its full-year net-new ARR growth outlook. Shares rose more than 20%.
Market Interpretation: Institutions see cybersecurity as one of the more rigid slices of AI spend. The Flex model improved expansion elasticity, and international revenue accelerated for a fifth consecutive quarter, showing growth is not solely dependent on large North American accounts. Analysts will watch whether margin expansion can coexist with high growth.
Investment Implications: Suitable as high-beta exposure to AI-security adoption; track net-new ARR and retention rates.

4. Tesla (TSLA) – Rises Nearly 3% With the Tech Rebound

Event Overview: Tesla rose about 2.4% to $354.25, outperforming some consumer-tech leaders. Markets also noted Trump’s executive order restricting certain foreign power equipment from the U.S. grid, which some analysts see as an indirect positive for domestic energy-storage and grid capabilities.
Market Interpretation: Institutions attribute the move more to repaired risk appetite and a return of tech beta than to a standalone fundamental inflection. Energy and grid policy add a narrative increment, but deliveries, gross margin and autonomous-driving commercialization remain the medium-term pricing core.
Investment Implications: Near-term trading remains tied to tech sentiment; the medium-term case still depends on energy-business contribution and execution.

5. Apple (AAPL) – Relatively Steady Ahead of the Launch Event

Event Overview: Apple closed slightly higher. The company has confirmed its autumn event for early morning September 10 Beijing time, with markets still pricing the first foldable iPhone and the iPhone 18 Pro series.
Market Interpretation: In a session dominated by Nvidia and software spikes, Apple’s smaller gain shows capital chasing higher-beta themes. Institutions still regard it as the more stable cash-flow allocation inside technology and remain focused on pricing and the replacement cycle.
Investment Implications: Suitable as a relatively defensive core holding in tech; watch launch pricing and first-sale data.

IV. Market Project Updates

  1. Bitcoin reclaimed $80,000. Spot ETFs recorded about $2.8 billion of cumulative net inflows over eight sessions, with IBIT contributing the bulk.
  2. Bernstein continues to position Bitcoin as a core “debasement-trade” asset and maintains a $300,000 year-end 2029 target.
  3. Glassnode said August 19 produced the largest single-day short liquidation in its records. The $82,000–$86,000 zone remains key resistance and a liquidation band.
  4. Reports that Nvidia is in talks to acquire open-source model platform Hugging Face for about $12.9 billion reinforced the narrative of its expansion into the model ecosystem.
  5. Strive CEO Matt Cole said the next year may be difficult, but that over the following four to five years Bitcoin could comfortably exceed $500,000. He argued the dollar is depreciating and that scarce assets such as gold, silver and Bitcoin should be viewed as wealth-preservation tools rather than measured in today’s dollar terms.

V. Today’s Market Calendar

Data Release Schedule

22:00 United States Warsh Jackson Hole keynote ⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐
Evening United States Chicago PMI; University of Michigan final consumer sentiment ⭐⭐⭐
 
 

Key Event Preview

  • Warsh speech: 22:00 August 28 (UTC+8). Focus on the 2% inflation target, communication framework, and fiscal/debt issues—not on whether he names a September hike.
  • Preliminary non-farm employment benchmark revision: Tests the scale of labor-market data revisions.
  • Digestion of the Nvidia move: Watch whether gains broaden beyond the mega-cap itself.

Institutional Views

Investment-bank analysts argue that Nvidia’s beat and unusually long-dated guidance have materially repaired the AI-demand narrative, while Salesforce and CrowdStrike show that “software growth stall” pricing moved too far, too fast. Warsh’s Jackson Hole debut remains the macro centerpiece; markets care more about whether he can produce an anti-inflation roadmap than about a one-off hawkish or dovish label. Geopolitically, the U.S. refusal to return to the June Iran understanding has put a floor under oil and made sticky-inflation concerns harder to fade. Crypto has reclaimed $80,000 on ETF inflows and a short squeeze, but $82,000–$86,000 remains the key test. Overall strategy recommendation: treat tonight’s speech as a volatility catalyst; stay flexible on high-valuation growth stocks; and continue to track storage, optical communication, software monetization and power constraints as structural themes.

results.title: Marvell (MRVL.US) Q2 Earnings Preview: NVLink + Google Dual Ecosystem — Pricing Hasn’t Caught Up
results.content:
1. Investment Snapshot

Marvell reports this quarter’s results after the U.S. close on August 27, 2026. Buy-side expects revenue up about 15% sequentially (about +39.0% YoY), with next-quarter guidance around 12% QoQ — a bit above sell-side consensus. The bar is not that high. About half of surveyed funds do not expect a net new chip program this quarter. Single-quarter implied volatility is about 8.8%, well above NVIDIA. The stock has been out of favor for a long time, but the last five months — NVLink Fusion plus the full custom TPU deal with Google — have changed the fundamental backdrop. The real question this time is whether management can turn those partnerships into a verifiable revenue timeline.

2. Four Things to Watch

Focus 1: Why the market still won’t price it in early
Custom-chip revenue is tightly tied to large-customer project timing. There is a track record of splashy framework deals that fail to show up in quarterly numbers, so funds habitually discount partnership headlines. Versus Broadcom, Marvell lacks a comparable multi-customer ramp record. FY2028 forward P/E is about 35x — well above the teens for the sector — and the valuation is widely seen as having already run ahead of the story. Some active money previously rode passive inflows from index inclusion, then cut after the rebound. Positioning is light and expectations are low.

Focus 2: Has the NVIDIA ecosystem slot moved from narrative to orders?
At the end of March, NVIDIA brought Marvell into its AI ecosystem via NVLink Fusion: custom XPUs, NVLink-compatible scale-up networking, plus a silicon-photonics collaboration. NVIDIA also invested about $2 billion. That puts Marvell on the general-purpose GPU interconnect chain as well. The call needs to confirm whether related products are already in guidance — or still just ecosystem narrative.

Focus 3: Don’t read the Google deal’s “$120 billion scale” as backlog
The Google agreement disclosed August 19 and signed July 29 covers custom chips across the TPU ecosystem (inference accelerators, memory controllers, NICs, memory interfaces, near-memory compute). Marvell issued Google about 58.97 million warrants at a $206.58 strike, total size about $12.2 billion; full exercise would give Google about 7% ownership. Warrants vest on cumulative purchases: one tranche for every $500 million purchased, 240 tranches in total, corresponding to a $120 billion cumulative purchase scale by FY2033. That number is a vesting cap, not an order book. Institutions estimate the deal implies about $20 billion of business volume. Versus buy-side FY2027 total-revenue expectations of about $12 billion, the upside is large — but it has to be delivered by a ramp schedule.

Focus 4: Qualitative comments will matter more than this quarter’s growth
The numerical bar is not high. What actually prices the stock is three things: when Google revenue starts contributing (warrant vesting starts counting from FY2027 Q3 — that start date is already close); whether commentary on Microsoft Maia and other existing programs turns more constructive; and whether electro-optical interconnect, CXL and other adjacent businesses get quantified into guidance. If management only repeats the framework and gives no cadence, high volatility plus a 35x multiple leaves plenty of downside.

3. Risks and Opportunities

Upside catalysts:

  • A Google revenue ramp schedule, plus an upward revision to next-quarter or medium-term guidance
  • Stronger commentary on Microsoft Maia and existing large-customer programs, showing this is not a single-narrative story
  • Electro-optical interconnect, CXL and other adjacent businesses entering quantifiable guidance, reinforcing the “dual ecosystem” premium

Downside risks:

  • Vague comments on Google incremental revenue; the market keeps treating the deal as an option, not revenue
  • No net new programs this quarter, reinforcing the “announcement hot, delivery slow” custom-chip stigma
  • At 8.8% implied vol, expectation-gap trading cuts both ways; multiple compression can outrun fundamental improvement

4. Trading Implications

Bull case: With expectations low and positioning light, if the ramp timeline and existing-program commentary both turn concrete, the market may re-rate Marvell’s dual-supply-chain slot in both the GPU camp and the ASIC camp.

Bear case: Partnerships stay at the framework layer, or the warrant structure is read as dilution first and orders second — the stock can gap down hard on earnings night.

Key data points:

  • This-quarter revenue: is sequential growth close to ~15% (about +39.0% YoY)
  • Next-quarter guidance: does sequential growth reach ~12%
  • Google-related revenue start date, vesting cadence, and quantification in guidance
  • Microsoft Maia and net new chip programs

Whether electro-optical interconnect / CXL enter guidance

Trading levels (based on the Aug 26 close of about $245.11; after-hours once poked about $253–256)

  • Resistance: $251–253, $258–262, $270–275
  • Support: $236–238, $228–230, $220–222, $211–216
  • Beat: A hold and break above $251–253 opens $258–265; a pullback to $245–248 can be used as a dip-buy zone
  • Miss: A break below $236–238 could probe $228–230, with $220 or $211–216 as the next areas to watch

 

How to play it: Light or flat positioning can treat the payoff as asymmetric, but this is not a setup to go full size into the call. If already heavy, don’t add leverage ahead of the print. The deal’s value depends on the 240 warrant tranches vesting as purchases accumulate — not on one candle that night.

results.title: NVIDIA FY2027 Q2 Earnings Highlights: Revenue Doubles YoY to $96.2 Billion; Data Center Up 117%; Next-Year Guidance Implies ~70% Growth
results.content:
Key Takeaways

NVIDIA reported FY2027 Q2 revenue (quarter ended July 26, 2026) of $96.221 billion, up 106% year over year and 18% quarter over quarter. That beat analyst estimates by more than 4% and came in about $5.2 billion above the midpoint of the company’s prior Q2 guidance of $91.0 billion.

Non-GAAP adjusted EPS was $2.22, up 120% YoY and above the $2.09 consensus by nearly 6%.

Data center revenue was $89.0 billion (official figure $89.023 billion), up 117% YoY and accounting for about 92.5% of total revenue.

The company guided FY2027 Q3 revenue to a midpoint of $108.0 billion (±2%), implying nearly 90% YoY growth and the first quarter above $100 billion. Gross margin guidance midpoint, however, stepped down to 74.0%. Guidance “does not assume any data center compute revenue from China.”

On the earnings call, management guided FY2028 revenue growth of about 70%, well above the roughly 45% analyst expectation, and said Amazon AWS will deploy an additional 2 million GPUs in 2027–2028. After hours the stock initially dropped about 4%, then turned higher after the call and was up nearly 5% at one point. Shares had already risen more than 10% in the month leading into the report.

Detailed Breakdown

1. Overall revenue and profit

  • Revenue: $96.221 billion, +106% YoY, +18% QoQ; highest YoY growth rate since FY2025 Q2.
  • Prior Q2 revenue guidance midpoint was $91.0 billion; actual result exceeded that by about $5.2 billion.
  • Non-GAAP net income: $53.954 billion, +118% YoY, +18% QoQ.
  • Non-GAAP EPS: $2.22 vs. $2.09 expected.
  • Non-GAAP operating income: $63.956 billion, +124% YoY, above the $61.19 billion analyst estimate; operating margin about 66%.
  • GAAP net income: $59.688 billion, +126% YoY.
  • GAAP EPS: $2.46. GAAP exceeded non-GAAP mainly because the quarter included about $7.77 billion of net gains on equity securities (official figure $7.771 billion), which are excluded from non-GAAP profit.
  • GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were both 75.0%, roughly in line with expectations; up about 2.6 and 2.5 percentage points YoY respectively, and essentially flat QoQ.
  • Non-GAAP operating expenses: $8.232 billion, below the $8.32 billion estimate.
  • GAAP operating expenses: $8.408 billion, +55% YoY, +10% QoQ.
  • Operating cash flow for the quarter: $24.077 billion. Working-capital use rose: accounts receivable increased $22.346 billion, inventory $5.784 billion, and prepaid and other assets $5.497 billion.
  • About $26 billion was returned to shareholders in the quarter (buybacks and dividends). Next-quarter cash dividend is $0.25 per share; record date September 10, 2026; payment date October 1, 2026.
Metric FY2027 Q2 FY2027 Q1 FY2026 Q2 QoQ YoY
Revenue $96.221B $81.615B $46.743B +18% +106%
GAAP gross margin 75.0% 74.9% 72.4% +0.1 ppt +2.6 ppt
Non-GAAP gross margin 75.0% 75.0% 72.5% Flat +2.5 ppt
GAAP operating income $63.734B $53.536B $28.440B +19% +124%
Non-GAAP operating income $63.956B $53.783B $28.541B +19% +124%
GAAP net income $59.688B $58.321B $26.422B +2% +126%
Non-GAAP net income $53.954B $45.548B $24.763B +18% +118%
GAAP diluted EPS $2.46 $2.39 $1.08 +3% +128%
Non-GAAP diluted EPS $2.22 $1.87 $1.01 +19% +120%
 
 

2. Data center performance

  • Data center revenue: $89.0 billion (official $89.023 billion), +117% YoY, +18% QoQ, above analyst estimates of roughly $85.8–85.9 billion by nearly 4%.
  • About 92.5% of total company revenue; the business remains tightly tied to the global AI infrastructure buildout.
  • Growth was driven mainly by the Blackwell Ultra infrastructure r Blackwell still accounted for the majority of system shipments.
  • Hyperscale revenue: $48.71 billion, +102% YoY, +13% QoQ, above the $43.55 billion estimate.
  • Compute Networking: $88.3 billion, above the $84.69 billion estimate.
  • ACIE (AI cloud, industrial and enterprise): $40.31 billion, +138% YoY, +25% QoQ, but below the $41.96 billion market estimate. Official explanation: growth came from AI-native customers, enterprises, sovereign customers, and hyperscalers using AI cloud.
  • Data center Hopper product shipments to China were less than 1% of data center revenue in the quarter.
  • CEO Jensen Huang: “AI has reached an inflection point. It is doing useful work. Tokens are becoming productive and profitable. Compute is now revenue.”
  • A year ago, buildout was driven mainly by one AI lab. Today multiple frontier labs are expanding in parallel, the open-source model ecosystem is thriving, and physical AI is starting to go live.
  • The Vera Rubin platform has entered full-scale production. Racks are already running at partners including CoreWeave, Google Cloud, Microsoft Azure, Oracle Cloud Infrastructure, and Nebius. Management expects Rubin to account for about 20% of Q3 data center revenue.

3. Other segments

  • Edge Computing revenue: $7.2 billion (official $7.198 billion), +27% YoY, +13% QoQ, above the $6.61 billion estimate. Covers RTX, Windows on-device AI, robotics, autonomous driving, and is core to the “physical AI” narrative, but remains far smaller than data center.
  • By reported segment: Compute Networking $88.299 billion; Graphics $7.922 billion.
  • Structurally, NVIDIA remains highly dependent on data center in the near term. Edge/graphics is growing but is not yet large enough to change the revenue mix.
Market platform FY2027 Q2 FY2027 Q1 FY2026 Q2 QoQ YoY
Data Center $89.023B $75.246B $41.096B +18% +117%
of which: Hyperscale $48.710B $43.050B $24.168B +13% +102%
of which: ACIE $40.313B $32.196B $16.928B +25% +138%
Edge Computing $7.198B $6.369B $5.647B +13% +27%
Total $96.221B $81.615B $46.743B +18% +106%
 
 

Note: The company changed market-platform reporting in FY2027 Q1 and restated comparative periods. In Q2 it also reclassified one customer from ACIE to Hyperscale and restated prior periods.

4. Supply, purchase commitments, and “AI factory” expansion

  • Management stressed that demand is still accelerating, but supply is the bottleneck. CFO Colette Kress said demand continues to accelerate at current scale and customer forecasts point to a doubling of growth next year, but the company is “supply constrained.” Huang said true demand is well above 70%; if supply were unconstrained, growth would be higher. The broader supply chain is tight, with shortages in memory and other critical components.
  • Purchase commitments to suppliers rose to $279 billion from $119 billion last quarter, driven mainly by memory purchases.
  • 10-Q disclosure: supply and capacity commitments of about $279 billion; total future commitments across supply, cloud, data centers, equity investments, and capex of about $366 billion, plus about $36 billion of AI-cloud-related commitments.
  • On the call: the top five hyperscalers’ capex is expected to approach $800 billion in 2026 and about $1.3 trillion in 2027; cloud-industry backlog already exceeds $2 trillion.
  • NVIDIA is shifting from selling individual GPUs to system-level delivery of full racks, networking, CPUs, software, and deployment solutions. Rubin is not a single chip; it is an “AI factory” architecture that includes Vera CPU, Rubin GPU, Spectrum-6 networking, BlueField, security, storage, software toolchain, and the DSX platform.
  • The company is trying to address bottlenecks in power, land, data-center shells, networking, cooling, and long-term financing at the same time. It has formed strategic partnerships with Apollo, BlackRock, Blackstone, Brookfield, Goldman Sachs, and KKR, aiming to mobilize more than $500 billion of third-party capital for AI infrastructure. It has also locked land, power, and building-shell capacity with SB Energy at the Ohio PORTS-Pike campus.
  • Responding to “circular financing” questions, Kress said frontier labs such as OpenAI “will become the largest technology companies in history,” face a compute-access bottleneck, and that NVIDIA is providing capital support. “We understand the scale of this support… the capital we put in will generate excellent equity returns.”
Item Amount / basis Notes
Supplier commitments $279B Sharp rise from $119B last quarter, mainly memory purchases
Total future commitments (supply / cloud / data center / equity / capex, etc.) ~$366B 10-Q basis
Separately listed AI-cloud-related commitments ~$36B 10-Q basis
Targeted third-party AI infrastructure capital >$500B Call / media basis; not company on-balance-sheet capex guidance
 
 

The original material did not include an item-by-item capex comparison versus AMD, Broadcom, or other chip peers, so no such peer figures are invented here.

5. Next-quarter guidance and FY2028 outlook

FY2027 Q3 guidance:

  • Revenue $108.0 billion ±2%, or about $105.8–110.2 billion; YoY growth about 85.6%–93.3%, midpoint about 89.5%.
  • Above Street consensus (Futu source cited ~$105.15 billion; other compilations roughly $104–105 billion). Even the low end of the range would put the company in the $100 billion-per-quarter club.
  • Guidance explicitly “does not assume any data center compute revenue from China.”
  • GAAP and non-GAAP gross margin midpoint both 74.0% ±50 bps, below the ~75% analyst expectation.
  • GAAP opex about $9.2 billion; non-GAAP about $9.0 billion.
  • Full-year FY2027 GAAP and non-GAAP tax rate expected at 16.0%–18.0% (excluding discrete items and major tax-law changes).
  • Sequentially, the $108.0 billion midpoint is up about 12% from Q2’s $96.2 billion, slower than Q2’s 18% sequential growth.
  • Management said Q3 sequential growth will be driven mainly by ACIE within data center; hyperscale growth is expected to re-accelerate in Q4 and FY2028 as Vera Rubin supply ramps.

Longer-term profit and growth path:

  • Gross margin is expected to bottom around 71%–72% in Q4 and stabilize around 72%–73% in FY2028. The company plans to implement price increases starting in the first quarter of the next fiscal year.
  • FY2028 revenue is expected to grow about 70%, well above the roughly 45% analyst expectation. This is a supply-constrained outlook; the supply bottleneck is expected to last at least through the end of FY2028.
  • Expanded AWS partnership: on top of the existing plan for about 1 million GPUs, an additional 2 million GPUs will be deployed in 2027–2028 (covering Blackwell Ultra, Rubin, and Rubin Ultra), along with Vera CPUs (some integrated with Rubin, some standalone).
Guidance item Company guidance Street / source estimates Key difference
Q3 revenue $108.0B ±2% ~$104.0–105.15B About 3%–4% above consensus, but short of the most optimistic ~$112B
Q3 gross margin 74.0% ±50 bps ~75% Slightly below expectations
Q3 non-GAAP opex ~$9.0B — Continues to rise from Q2’s $8.232B
China data center compute revenue Not included in guidance — Potential upside, but not a certainty
FY2028 revenue growth ~70% ~45% The key point that flipped sentiment after the call
 
 

6. Market context and investor concerns

  • The core issue was not whether the quarter beat sell-side consensus, but whether it cleared the higher bar already priced in by buyers. Shares had already risen more than 10% in the month before the report; the market was trading the size of the beat.
  • The initial after-hours drop of about 4% was triggered by Q3 gross-margin guidance coming in slightly light; revenue guidance beating consensus but not the most bullish range; and China data center compute being excluded from guidance, so any recovery could not be treated as a locked-in upward revision.
  • The stock turned up nearly 5% after the call, driven by the ~70% FY2028 growth guide, the additional 2 million GPUs for AWS, and management’s emphasis that demand is still accelerating and AI has reached a “compute is revenue” inflection.
  • Structural concern: the beat this quarter was driven mainly by hyperscale customers. ACIE came in below expectations, suggesting enterprise, industrial, and some AI-cloud expansion is slower than previously hoped.
  • Margin pressure comes from early Rubin production costs and yields, rising supply-chain costs for HBM / advanced packaging / substrates, and a richer mix of full-rack system deliveries.
  • The balance sheet is expanding quickly: total assets rose from $206.8 billion on January 25, 2026 to $320.3 billion on July 26, 2026. Accounts receivable stood at $63.059 billion and inventory at $31.575 billion; higher working-capital use is already showing up in free cash flow.
  • Ecosystem investments versus the core business remain in focus: nearly $7.8 billion of net equity-securities gains boosted GAAP profit this quarter, while capital support for labs and the ecosystem has been labeled “circular financing” by some in the market. Management denied that characterization and stressed equity returns.
  • China remains uncertain: China Hopper shipments were under 1% of data center revenue this quarter, and forward guidance fully excludes China data center compute revenue.
  • Capital return did not include a more aggressive commitment beyond existing authorizations. The company said it will increase return of excess free cash flow after strategic uses.

I. Hot News Highlights

Federal Reserve Dynamics

July PCE Runs Hot; Walsh’s Jackson Hole Speech Arrives Tonight

  • U.S. July PCE rose 3.7% year-over-year and 0.2% month-over-month, both above expectations, reconfirming inflation stickiness.
  • The Jackson Hole global central-bank symposium opens Thursday ET; Fed Chair Kevin Walsh delivers the keynote on Friday.
  • CME data still show holding rates unchanged in September as the baseline scenario, but the hot inflation print makes hike pricing difficult to fully fade.
    Market Impact: Hotter PCE weighed on near-term risk appetite. Walsh’s speech is the week’s most important policy-communication window and will directly affect term premiums and growth-stock pricing.

International Commodities

Trump Says No Timetable for Iran Talks; Diplomacy and Pressure Run in Parallel

  • In an interview, President Trump said he has “no timetable and is in no hurry” for Iran to return to the negotiating table, while arguing Iran faces severe inflation and a collapsing economy.
  • Energy Secretary Wright said Washington prefers a diplomatic solution but would destroy Iran’s nuclear facilities if necessary.
  • Iranian President Pezeshkian responded that current U.S. economic pressure will not succeed.
    Market Impact: Expectations of a rapid geopolitical thaw have cooled, giving oil some support. Reassessment risk around the inflation path has risen, increasing near-term commodity volatility.

Macroeconomic Policy

Data-Center Delay Risk Rises; White House Advances Drug-Pricing Deals

  • Kimmeridge co-founder Ben Dell estimates that as many as half of planned U.S. data centers could be delayed or canceled because of political opposition, litigation and physical-infrastructure constraints.
  • The White House plans a new round of “most-favored-nation” drug-pricing agreements with several mid-sized biotech firms, covering Medicaid discounts.
  • President Trump signed an executive order restricting certain foreign-made large power-system equipment from entering the U.S. grid.
    Market Impact: The pace of AI infrastructure deployment faces real-world constraints, drawing attention to power and domestic-equipment themes. Drug-pricing agreements create a policy variable for related pharmaceutical names.

II. Market Review

Commodities Forex Performance

  • Spot Gold: Approx. $4,605/oz, +0.23%

Driver Analysis: The hotter July PCE print reinforced the sticky-inflation narrative and provided some support for precious metals. Trump’s comment that there is no timetable for Iran talks prevented geopolitical premiums from fading further, helping oil stabilize. Institutional views hold that near-term commodities are jointly driven by “hot inflation + geopolitical uncertainty,” with the linkage running from a hotter PCE → repricing of real rates and the policy path → gold attracting haven and store-of-value demand, while oil is underpinned by geopolitics.

Performance Summary Driver Analysis: Hotter PCE left the three major indexes slightly lower as capital stayed cautious ahead of Nvidia’s report. Storage and optical-communication sectors continued to strengthen, and cybersecurity stocks advanced broadly. Nvidia’s after-hours beat and FY2028 growth guidance of about 70% significantly lifted sentiment, pushing tech futures higher. Individual-stock divergence shifted from “macro caution” toward “company-level fundamental validation.”

Sector Movers Observation

Storage – Continued Strength

  • Representative stocks: Western Digital up more than 4%; Seagate Technology up more than 3%; SanDisk up more than 1%; Micron Technology slightly higher.

Optical Communication – Sharp Gains

  • Representative stocks: Lumentum up more than 6%; Ciena up more than 4%; Corning up nearly 4%; Coherent up more than 2%.
  • Drivers: Demand for high-speed AI interconnect remains intact, and the recovery from the prior correction continued.

Cybersecurity – Broad Advance

  • Representative stocks: Okta jumped nearly 21% after hours; CrowdStrike, Cloudflare and Datadog rose more than 2%.
  • Drivers: Improved earnings and order expectations, plus a rotation into defensive software amid macro uncertainty.

III. In-Depth US Equity Analysis

1. Nvidia (NVDA) – Large Q2 Beat and Rare Long-Dated Guidance

Event Overview: Nvidia reported FY2027 Q2 revenue of $96.2 billion, up 106% year-over-year, and adjusted EPS of $2.22, up 120%. Data-center revenue reached $89.0 billion, up 117% and above estimates. GAAP and non-GAAP gross margins were both 75.0%. CFO Colette Kress unusually guided FY2028 revenue growth of about 70% versus prior analyst expectations of roughly 44%, adding that the outlook would be “much higher” without supply constraints. CEO Jensen Huang said demand growth is approaching 100% and that the 70% figure is a conservative estimate based on current supply capacity. Shares rose more than 4% after hours.
Market Interpretation: Institutions view the print as a strong validation of AI-demand durability. Giving high-growth guidance a full year early is rare and implies improved order visibility; the “supply-constrained” qualifier also signals that pricing power and capacity bottlenecks remain. Analysts will watch whether the guide can be delivered, whether customer capex begins to diverge, and whether margins hold as memory costs rise.
Investment Implications: The medium-term thesis is strengthened by demand validation, but valuations already discount part of the optimism. Monitor supply-release cadence and next-quarter data-center guidance.

2. Apple (AAPL) – Foldable Launch Set for September 10

Event Overview: Apple confirmed its autumn launch event for 1:00 a.m. Beijing time on September 10, under the slogan “Surprise and Shine.” Markets expect the first foldable iPhone as well as iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, with faster chips and longer battery life. The event will be new CEO John Ternus’s first major product showcase.
Market Interpretation: Institutions see the foldable as the start of a new hardware-innovation cycle that could lift replacement demand and the services ecosystem. Analysts are focused on pricing, yields and initial shipment scale, and regard the event itself as near-term sentiment support.
Investment Implications: Suitable as a relatively defensive technology allocation; track new-product pricing and first-sale data.

3. Meta (META) – Settlement of Up to About $18 Billion With Multiple States

Event Overview: Meta agreed to pay up to about $18 billion to settle landmark litigation with multiple U.S. states over social media’s impact on minors.
Market Interpretation: Institutions argue that although the one-time payment is large, it removes a long-running legal overhang and allows the market to refocus on advertising and AI. Near-term profits may be hit, but medium-term regulatory tail risk is reduced.
Investment Implications: Watch the settlement’s effect on free cash flow and buyback cadence, as well as any subsequent change in the regulatory backdrop.

4. Lumentum (LITE) – Optical Communication Continues to Lead

Event Overview: Lumentum rose more than 6% as the optical-communication group strengthened, with Ciena, Corning and Coherent also advancing.
Market Interpretation: Institutions believe demand for 800G/1.6T optical modules in AI data centers remains in an expansion phase, giving the rebound from the prior correction fundamental support. Order visibility and capacity ramps remain key observation points.
Investment Implications: High-beta thematic exposure suitable for tracking optical-module momentum and capex delivery.

5. Okta (OKTA) – Sharp After-Hours Rally in Cybersecurity
